questions.question: What best describes artificial intelligence?
options: Only systems that learn from labeled examples
Only multilayer neural-network systems
Computer systems performing tasks associated with intelligence
Only systems that generate new language
questions.explanation: AI is a broad name for computer systems that do tasks linked with intelligence. Examples include recognizing speech, finding patterns and generating text.

questions.question: Which event is associated with the formal founding of AI?
options: The 1986 connectionism books
The 1997 Deep Blue match
The 2012 ImageNet competition
The 1956 Dartmouth workshop
questions.explanation: The notes associate the field's founding with Dartmouth and John McCarthy.

questions.question: What distinguishes symbolic AI?
options: Explicit human-written rules and symbols
Weights adjusted from labeled examples
Categories discovered in unlabeled data
Action values updated from rewards
questions.explanation: Symbolic systems make rules inspectable, but depend on anticipating relevant situations.

questions.question: Why can a symbolic clinical tool be brittle?
options: Its rules automatically adapt to every unseen case
Its rules may not cover unfamiliar situations
Its transparency prevents any clinical error
Its rules are learned without human knowledge
questions.explanation: Rules work within the situations their designers anticipated.

questions.question: How is knowledge typically represented in subsymbolic AI?
options: Explicit rules elicited from clinicians
A readable chain of logical propositions
Numerical weights learned from examples
A manually written list of category definitions
questions.explanation: The model learns many numbers called weights. Its knowledge is spread across these numbers, so the reasons behind an answer can be hard to inspect.

questions.question: An expert labels recordings typical or disordered. Which learning approach uses these examples?
options: Unsupervised learning
Supervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Manual rule execution only
questions.explanation: Supervised learning uses examples with target labels.

questions.question: A system groups children by similar performance without diagnostic labels. This is what type of learning?
options: Supervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Unsupervised learning
Backward chaining
questions.explanation: Unsupervised methods discover structure in unlabeled data.

questions.question: A system improves actions through rewards. Which learning approach is this?
options: Reinforcement learning
Rule-based inference
Static transcription
Supervised classification
questions.explanation: Reinforcement learning uses feedback on actions rather than correct labels for every example.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a training set?
options: To learn model parameters
To produce an independent final performance estimate
To confirm performance after deployment only
To select the best score after repeated test submissions
questions.explanation: Training examples are used during learning.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a held-out test set?
options: To select weights through repeated feedback
To replace the need for a training set
To assess performance on unseen examples
To establish that a model understands every case
questions.explanation: The model has not learned from these examples. Testing on them checks whether it can handle something new.

questions.question: Why does repeatedly adjusting a model to improve its test score undermine evaluation?
options: It converts supervised learning into reinforcement learning
It removes any need for external validation
It makes the test set more representative automatically
The test set begins influencing development
questions.explanation: If developers keep changing the model to suit the test, the test is no longer an independent check. The score may look better than real-world performance.

questions.question: What does a simple perceptron do?
options: Selects the largest raw input without weighting
Thresholds a weighted sum of inputs
Predicts a word by matching it to a dictionary definition
Updates every input to the same numerical value
questions.explanation: Each input is multiplied by a weight. The perceptron adds the results and checks whether the total reaches a cutoff.

questions.question: Which sequence describes a layered neural network?
options: Input, output, hidden layers
Hidden layers, input, output
Input, hidden layers, output
Input, training labels, hidden layers only
questions.explanation: Input brings information in. Hidden layers process it. The output gives the result.

questions.question: How do the notes define a deep network?
options: A network with exactly one hidden layer
Any network trained on a large dataset
A network with more than one hidden layer
Any network with several output categories
questions.explanation: Depth refers to layered computational processing, not file size.

questions.question: What does back-propagation use to guide weight updates?
options: Error at the network output
Only the number of layers chosen by the designer
Only the predicted category without its error
Only the input signal before any comparison
questions.explanation: The model compares its answer with the expected answer. Error information travels backward to help adjust the weights.

questions.question: What is an activation map in a ConvNet?
options: A list of final category predictions for every patient
The table of training and test labels
A grid of responses to a visual feature
The sequence of all weight updates over training
questions.explanation: Each grid records where a particular feature was detected. Reusing the same weights lets the model look for that feature in different places.

questions.question: Which is an example of natural language processing?
options: Translating or summarizing language
Classifying a voice sample using jitter alone
Detecting an object in a photograph
Learning a robot's movement from rewards
questions.explanation: NLP deals computationally with human language.

questions.question: What distinguishes generative AI?
options: It creates new content
It produces only predefined category labels
It only retrieves unchanged records from storage
It guarantees that generated content is factual
questions.explanation: Generative means creating content. Examples include new text, images and speech; new content is not automatically true.

questions.question: How does the notes' simplified account describe an LLM generating text?
options: Selecting only independently verified factual statements
Applying a fixed clinical rule to every case
Predicting likely next pieces of language
Retrieving a complete answer unchanged from one source
questions.explanation: The model builds text by predicting likely next pieces. A likely continuation can sound good and still be wrong.

questions.question: What does generalization mean?
options: Matching training examples with minimal error
Performing well on new unseen data
Choosing settings that maximize a test score after repeated tuning
Producing a clear explanation for every prediction
questions.explanation: A useful model must handle examples it did not train on. Doing that well is called generalization.

questions.question: Which sequence represents a typical clinical AI pipeline?
options: Input data, feature extraction, prediction
Prediction, feature extraction, input data
Feature extraction, final diagnosis, consent
Training labels, care plan, input data
questions.explanation: Clinical AI transforms data into features and outputs that require interpretation.

questions.question: What is accuracy?
options: The proportion of flagged cases truly affected
The proportion of affected cases detected
The proportion of unaffected cases cleared
The proportion of all cases classified correctly
questions.explanation: Count all correct classifications, then divide by all cases tested. Accuracy alone can hide which kinds of errors occurred.

questions.question: What is sensitivity also called?
options: Precision
Recall
Prompt dependence
Specificity
questions.explanation: Recall and sensitivity mean the same thing here: how many genuinely affected children the screener catches.

questions.question: What does specificity measure?
options: The proportion of unaffected cases correctly cleared
The total number of training examples
The proportion of affected cases detected
The proportion of positive predictions that are correct
questions.explanation: Start with children who do not have the difficulty. Specificity is the share correctly given a negative result.

questions.question: What does precision measure?
options: How many affected cases are detected
How many features are extracted
How many flagged cases truly have the difficulty
How many unaffected cases are cleared
questions.explanation: Start with everyone the tool flags. Precision is the share of those flagged people who really have the difficulty.

questions.question: What does AUC broadly describe in the notes?
options: The proportion of flagged cases truly affected
Overall separation between two groups
The percentage of model predictions made with confidence
The proportion of unaffected cases correctly cleared at one threshold
questions.explanation: AUC describes how well the model separates the groups across thresholds. It does not by itself show that using the tool improves care.

questions.question: Why prioritize sensitivity in an early screening tool?
options: To maximize specificity even if more children are missed
To remove the need for follow-up assessment
To reduce missed children needing assessment
To guarantee that every flagged child has the difficulty
questions.explanation: Missing an affected child can delay access to early support.

questions.question: What should follow a positive screening result?
options: A final diagnosis based solely on the model score
A full clinical assessment
Immediate service eligibility based only on the flag
A repeat screen used as the only diagnostic evidence
questions.explanation: Screening flags risk and does not replace comprehensive assessment.

questions.question: What did the DLD example in the notes involve?
options: Only English-speaking adults
Cypriot Greek children
Only people with Parkinson's disease
Only written legal documents
questions.explanation: The example demonstrates that evidence is tied to a particular population.

questions.question: Which features mattered more in the cited DLD example?
options: Perception features
Demographic features alone
Production features
Caregiver-report features alone
questions.explanation: This is a study-specific result reported in the lecture notes, not a universal rule.

questions.question: The notes report about 75% accuracy for an autism-related model using what input?
options: Only acoustic measures such as jitter and shimmer
Only receptive-language test scores
Transcript features such as mean length of utterance
Only demographic and appointment data
questions.explanation: The reported result is tied to the example study and its dataset.

questions.question: Why may ordinary ASR perform poorly on disordered speech?
options: ASR is designed to classify diagnoses rather than transcribe speech
Disordered speech always has less background noise
More training data from typical adults necessarily fixes the mismatch
Its training data may underrepresent that speech
questions.explanation: Training examples influence which speech patterns a recognizer handles well.

questions.question: What improved ASR in the notes' example?
options: Testing repeatedly on the same conversational samples
Increasing the amount of typical adult speech only
Removing disordered examples to standardize the dataset
Adding conversational disordered-speech samples to training
questions.explanation: Relevant training examples can improve recognition for an underrepresented population.

questions.question: Which set contains voice acoustic measures listed in the notes?
options: Jitter, shimmer, spectral tilt and harmonic-to-noise ratio
Mean length of utterance, vocabulary diversity, syntax and semantics
Sensitivity, specificity, precision and AUC
Independent accuracy, supported accuracy, prompt dependence and NR
questions.explanation: These measures describe aspects of the voice signal.

questions.question: The notes report 88% classification accuracy for which comparison?
options: People who stutter versus controls
Children with DLD versus typically developing children
People with Parkinson's disease versus controls
Children at risk of later reading difficulty versus controls
questions.explanation: The 88% result belongs to a specific example and should not be generalized automatically.

questions.question: What Parkinson's voice-detection range is reported in the notes?
options: Roughly 85–90%
Exactly 100%
Exactly 50%
Roughly 20–25%
questions.explanation: This is the range reported by the notes, rather than an independently updated estimate.

questions.question: What benefit did the predictive multimodal AAC example report?
options: About 30% higher diagnostic accuracy
About 30% fewer clinicians needed for all care
About 30% better independent speech accuracy
About 30% less message construction time
questions.explanation: The example concerns message construction time in a particular framework.

questions.question: The Lexiland example reports which sensitivity and specificity?
options: 90% sensitivity and 76% specificity
100% sensitivity and 100% specificity
76% sensitivity and 90% specificity
50% sensitivity and 50% specificity
questions.explanation: The notes use these values to illustrate screening and triage trade-offs.

questions.question: What did improvement on untreated /r/ words illustrate in the remote-practice example?
options: Generalization beyond practiced items
Memorization limited to the trained word list
Transfer from screening directly to diagnosis
Evidence that clinician feedback is unnecessary
questions.explanation: Transfer to untreated words suggests learning beyond the exact practiced examples.

questions.question: Before applying a promising published tool locally, what matters most?
options: Only the strongest overall accuracy reported by the developers
Only validation on the original training population
Only whether its output matches clinical expectations in one case
Validation for similar ages, languages, dialects and disorders
questions.explanation: A good result in one study may not transfer to your patients. Check whether similar ages, languages, dialects and disorders were tested.

questions.question: Why can an AI system reproduce population bias?
options: Its numerical design automatically removes social inequalities
It learns patterns from unrepresentative data
Only deliberate discriminatory instructions can create bias
A large dataset guarantees equal subgroup representation
questions.explanation: Who is included in training affects who benefits and who may be harmed.

questions.question: An ASR system works well on standard speech but poorly on a regional dialect. What should be investigated?
options: Dialect representation and subgroup error rates
Only the pooled accuracy across all dialects
Only transcription speed on standard speech
Only the recognizer's average confidence score
questions.explanation: Aggregate scores can conceal unequal performance across dialects.

questions.question: Why can adult-trained ASR fail on children's speech?
options: Adult-trained models automatically normalize all developmental differences
Children's speech needs only a larger test set without retraining
Age-related speech characteristics may be underrepresented
Any error on children's speech proves a language disorder
questions.explanation: A mismatch between training and use populations can reduce performance.

questions.question: What is the concern about geographically concentrated clinical datasets?
options: Large datasets from a few places automatically represent every language
Geographic concentration makes subgroup testing unnecessary
A shared medical label guarantees identical local conditions
Performance may not generalize to other settings
questions.explanation: The notes highlight concentration in the US and China as a generalizability concern.

questions.question: A tool trained on monolingual English-speaking children is used with bilingual children. What is the central risk?
options: Guaranteed transfer because both groups include some English
Linguistic and cultural mismatch
A need to remove the child's other language from assessment
Evidence that bilingualism itself is a disorder
questions.explanation: Training context should be compared with the intended population.

questions.question: Why did using healthcare cost as a proxy for health need create bias in the notes' example?
options: Spending and health need are interchangeable measures
A cost target guarantees equal access to referrals
Spending can reflect unequal access rather than actual need
Removing race as an input prevents all proxy bias
questions.explanation: Healthcare spending can be lower because access is unequal, even when need is high. Using cost as if it were need can therefore produce unfair referrals.

questions.question: Which combination is recommended to mitigate bias?
options: A larger dataset, overall accuracy and no subgroup reporting
Removing demographic variables and assuming fairness
Representative data, subgroup audits and community involvement
Using the same threshold everywhere without auditing its effects
questions.explanation: Technical auditing and participation by affected communities complement each other.

questions.question: Why are voice recordings a privacy concern even after a name is removed?
options: Removing names always makes raw voice data anonymous
Only written transcripts can identify a person
A pseudonymous filename prevents all re-identification
The voice itself may help reveal identity
questions.explanation: A voice can be recognizable even without a written name. Removing names is useful, but does not guarantee that a recording is anonymous.

questions.question: What does data minimization mean?
options: Share only data needed for the task
Share the complete history to avoid every possible omission
Remove identifiers but retain all other data regardless of need
Retain all recordings because they might be useful later
questions.explanation: Share what the task actually needs. Extra records increase privacy exposure without necessarily making the result more useful.

questions.question: Which description best follows the notes' de-identification example?
options: School, parent phone and full name
Child A, age 5;2
National ID and appointment number
Full name, birth date and address
questions.explanation: The notes model a pseudonymous case with clinically relevant age information.

questions.question: What should happen before AI-assisted recording or transcription?
options: Obtain informed consent using an approved workflow
Record first and obtain consent only if the output is useful
Treat attendance at therapy as consent for every external AI use
Use a public tool before asking about institutional approval
questions.explanation: Clients and caregivers should understand how AI is used.

questions.question: Which tool choice follows the notes' privacy guidance?
options: Any tool that states it uses encryption, without institutional review
A personal account chosen for convenience alone
A public tool after removing only the client's first name
An institution-approved tool with secure storage
questions.explanation: Approval, security and institutional policy matter when handling clinical information.

questions.question: What role should children and neurodivergent clients have in data use?
options: Participation only after all data decisions are finalized
Responsibility for verifying the vendor's training process
Automatic exclusion from decisions to avoid burdening them
A meaningful voice in decisions affecting them
questions.explanation: Autonomy includes involving affected people appropriately.

questions.question: How should a learner interpret the notes' discussion of HIPAA?
options: As a substitute for local policy
As permission to share de-identified audio publicly
As a US framework whose applicability depends on context
As a universal law applying identically everywhere
questions.explanation: The notes explicitly caution against assuming universal applicability.

questions.question: If no AI-specific rule clearly fits a setting, what do the notes recommend?
options: Ignore professional obligations
Follow applicable local data rules and institutional policy
Treat the absence of an AI law as unrestricted permission
Follow only a vendor's advertising
questions.explanation: Existing privacy and professional duties remain relevant.

questions.question: Which WHO principle supports meaningful patient choice?
options: Transparency and explainability
Responsibility and accountability
Responsive and sustainable AI
Protect autonomy
questions.explanation: The notes list autonomy among the six WHO principles.

questions.question: Which WHO principle addresses understandable AI use?
options: Inclusiveness and equity
Autonomy alone
Responsiveness and sustainability
Transparency, explainability and intelligibility
questions.explanation: Users should be able to understand relevant aspects of system operation and output.

questions.question: Which WHO principle concerns unequal access and unfair performance?
options: Inclusiveness and equity
Transparency alone
Environmental sustainability alone
Accountability alone
questions.explanation: Fair access and performance are ethical concerns, not just technical details.

questions.question: Who remains accountable for care decisions when AI is used?
options: Only the patient
Only the software vendor
The clinician
The algorithm itself
questions.explanation: Using a tool does not transfer professional responsibility to it.

questions.question: Why does sustainability appear in AI ethics?
options: Large models always use fewer resources than small ones
A clinically useful system has no environmental impact
Large models can have energy and carbon costs
Sustainability concerns only the lifetime of a device
questions.explanation: The notes include responsive and sustainable AI among the ethical principles.

questions.question: Which description best characterizes a trustworthy AI tool?
options: High overall accuracy without subgroup or privacy checks
Valid, safe, secure, fair and privacy-protecting
Fluent output combined with a persuasive explanation
Fast output and a high training-set score
questions.explanation: A tool needs to do its intended job and protect people. A high accuracy score is only one part of that judgment.

questions.question: Which evidence most strongly supports clinical trust?
options: Representative validation with subgroup results and intended-use limits
Repeatedly optimized performance on the same test set
High accuracy on training examples alone
A vendor demonstration using selected successful cases
questions.explanation: Independent relevant evaluation is stronger than marketing or training performance.

questions.question: What is an AI hallucination?
options: A false negative from a clinical screener only
Confidently stated content that is false or unsupported
An explicitly acknowledged uncertainty
A correct statement expressed with low confidence
questions.explanation: The model fills a gap with something that sounds believable but is false or unsupported. Invented citations are one example.

questions.question: Which output is a warning sign of hallucination?
options: A clear marker that the transcript did not state a detail
A highly specific statistic without a traceable source
A specific finding linked to a verified original source
A calculation shown from the provided trial counts
questions.explanation: Specificity and fluency do not supply evidence.

questions.question: An AI supplies a journal citation that cannot be located. What should the clinician do?
options: Keep it if its title matches the clinical topic
Verify independently and remove or correct it if unsupported
Ask the same model to repeat it and treat repetition as verification
Assume a correctly formatted citation must exist
questions.explanation: References must be checked against real sources.

questions.question: Why can a persuasive explanation be unsafe?
options: It may raise trust without being accurate or checkable
Any explanation directly exposes the model's true internal process
Clinical plausibility proves the explanation is causally faithful
A longer explanation removes the need for source checking
questions.explanation: A convincing story about an answer may itself be wrong. A useful explanation should help you check the result, rather than simply make you trust it.

questions.question: What should a pilot audit compare before wider clinical use?
options: Only pooled accuracy without subgroup breakdown
Only agreement with one clinician in a selected successful case
Performance across relevant subgroups
Only speed relative to manual work
questions.explanation: Pilots can expose age, language or dialect performance differences.

questions.question: Should AI alone decide whether a child qualifies for services?
options: Yes, if a single accuracy figure is high
Yes, if the tool is free
No, eligibility needs appropriate clinical judgment
Yes, if the text is confident
questions.explanation: The notes warn against using AI output alone to withhold services or determine eligibility.

questions.question: What is automation bias?
options: A guaranteed reduction in error
Overreliance on automated output
A preference for handwritten notes
A balanced independent appraisal
questions.explanation: This means accepting an automated answer too readily. Keep comparing the output with the evidence instead of assuming the computer is right.

questions.question: In the appraisal routine, what does the Source check ask?
options: Does the output fit the clinician's preferred writing style?
Does the model give the same answer twice?
Does the answer sound professionally worded?
Can every fact and citation be verified?
questions.explanation: Source checking tests whether claims are traceable.

questions.question: What does the Accuracy check compare?
options: AI output with observations and client data
AI output with the model's own confidence alone
AI output with a generic example from another patient
AI output with the vendor's accuracy claim alone
questions.explanation: Clinical data provide a necessary basis for checking an output.

questions.question: What does the Bias check examine?
options: Possible errors linked to language, dialect or culture
Only the model's overall published accuracy
Only whether race is an explicit input
Only whether the same threshold is used for everyone
questions.explanation: A polished output may still be inappropriate for a particular population.

questions.question: What does the Scope check ask?
options: Is AI making judgments reserved for the clinician?
Whether the output is longer than the original transcript
Whether the draft follows the requested table format
Whether the tool predicts a label with high confidence
questions.explanation: Diagnosis and prognosis require professional clinical judgment.

questions.question: What does the Privacy check ask?
options: Whether the answer includes a statement about confidentiality
Whether the clinician removed only the client's first name
Whether all generated text uses clinical terminology
Was identifiable information kept out?
questions.explanation: Privacy must be checked throughout the workflow.

questions.question: What does the Usefulness check examine?
options: Whether output improves care or saves meaningful time
Whether it produces more text than a manual note
Whether it matches the vendor's demonstration
Whether it eliminates every need for review
questions.explanation: A tool should add practical value after review costs are considered.

questions.question: What should happen if an appraisal step is unresolved?
options: Assume the next model version will fix it
Ignore the uncertain section
Correct or discard the output before use
Sign it immediately
questions.explanation: Uncertainty should trigger verification or rejection of the draft.

questions.question: A system misses a child who truly has a difficulty. What is this error?
options: True positive
True negative
False negative
False positive
questions.explanation: A false negative is an affected case incorrectly classified as negative.

questions.question: A system flags a child who does not have the difficulty. What is this error?
options: True positive
False positive
False negative
True negative
questions.explanation: A false positive is a positive prediction for an unaffected case.

questions.question: A tool's reported accuracy falls when used in a new dialect group. What concept is most relevant?
options: Perfect calibration
Poor generalizability
Guaranteed validity
Improved representativeness
questions.explanation: The model learned from one kind of population, but the new group differs. Lower performance shows that its learning did not transfer well.

questions.question: Which question most directly addresses task clarity?
options: What data was it trained on?
What is the AI actually doing?
How accurate and validated is it?
Where does the SLP remain responsible?
questions.explanation: The slide deck asks users to clarify the actual computational task before trusting results.

questions.question: Why does a precise prompt generally reduce rework?
options: It makes the model's knowledge clinically validated
It prevents hallucinations without source checking
It replaces the need for developmentally appropriate review
It states the intended task and constraints clearly
questions.explanation: Specific instructions make the draft more likely to match the user's needs.

questions.question: Which set lists the six prompt components in the notes?
options: Role, task, context, format, constraints, examples
Name, address, diagnosis, password, payment, signature
Accuracy, AUC, sensitivity, specificity, recall, precision
Training, testing, deployment, billing, consent, audit
questions.explanation: Say who the AI should act as, what it should make, the relevant background, the layout, the limits and any examples.

questions.question: What does the Role component specify?
options: The perspective the AI should adopt
The requested output structure
The specific activity to create
The de-identified details of the case
questions.explanation: A role frames the desired style and professional perspective without granting actual expertise.

questions.question: Which instruction states a Task?
options: Avoid identifying information
Act as a paediatric SLP
Create a home-practice activity
Use a three-column table
questions.explanation: The task names the output or action requested.

questions.question: Which information belongs in Context?
options: The requested number of table columns
The desired professional perspective alone
De-identified age, language background and relevant needs
The maximum activity duration alone
questions.explanation: Context makes material appropriate to the case while protecting identity.

questions.question: Which instruction specifies Format?
options: Present ten words and three steps in a table
Act as an SLP
Work with a five-year-old
Avoid diagnosis
questions.explanation: Format tells the system how to organize the answer.

questions.question: Which is a prompt Constraint?
options: Use caregiver-friendly language and no diagnosis
Act as a paediatric speech-language pathologist
Create a home-practice activity
Use a table with ten target words
questions.explanation: Constraints set limits on the output.

questions.question: What is zero-shot prompting?
options: Giving the task without examples
Providing one worked example
Providing three worked examples
Repeating an answer until it sounds correct
questions.explanation: Zero-shot means no worked example is included. You describe the task and ask for an answer.

questions.question: What is few-shot prompting in the notes?
options: Providing no demonstration examples
Providing a small number of examples, such as one to three
Requesting several outputs without examples
Retraining a model on a complete dataset
questions.explanation: Few-shot means giving a few examples. The examples help show the kind of answer or style you want.

questions.question: What should a speech-sound prompt specify beyond the sound itself?
options: Only how many times the sound occurs across the whole list
Its target position, such as initial /s/
Only the maximum number of words in the response
Only the type of table to use
questions.explanation: Target position helps align word choices with the intended practice goal.

questions.question: Why include developmental level as well as age?
options: Chronological age automatically predicts every language skill
Developmental level determines whether consent is necessary
To match vocabulary and activity demands to the child
A stated age guarantees suitable vocabulary without checking
questions.explanation: Age alone may not capture the level of support or language complexity needed.

questions.question: What should linguistic context include?
options: Languages, dialect and familiar cultural references
Only the language preferred by the model
Only the language of the original textbook
Only the clinician's professional terminology
questions.explanation: Materials should fit the child's actual language environment.

questions.question: Why specify the audience and reading level?
options: Technical language is equally useful for all readers
Reading level determines whether statements are true
An audience label makes citation checking unnecessary
A caregiver may need different wording from a clinician
questions.explanation: The same information can require different presentation for different readers.

questions.question: Which prompt is more clinically usable?
options: Write anything long
Create a guaranteed cure
Make something about speech
Create a 15-minute initial /s/ activity with ten target words and caregiver tips
questions.explanation: The specific prompt states target, duration, quantity and audience.

questions.question: A draft uses unfamiliar cultural objects. What is a useful refinement?
options: Add more diagnostic claims
Insert the child's full name
Accept them because the grammar is correct
Replace them with familiar objects from the child's setting
questions.explanation: Follow-up prompts can improve contextual fit.

questions.question: What should be verified in generated target words?
options: Only that the requested number of words is present
Only that each item is a familiar noun
That the words are real and contain the intended target
Only that each word has the same syllable count
questions.explanation: A neat format does not ensure accurate phonological targeting.

questions.question: What is the best status for a first AI-generated activity?
options: A draft requiring refinement and verification
A validated intervention ready for use without checking
A clinical recommendation equivalent to a full assessment
A final activity once it matches the requested format
questions.explanation: The notes advise an iterative process followed by checking.

questions.question: What privacy rule applies during follow-up prompting?
options: Share the full record after one revision
Keep identifying details out at every step
Add identifiers if the draft seems generic
Only the first prompt needs de-identification
questions.explanation: Privacy duties continue through the entire conversation.

questions.question: A prompt says 'act as an expert.' What does this guarantee?
options: No guarantee of factual or clinical correctness
Validated clinical reasoning
Accurate citations in every answer
Institutional approval
questions.explanation: A role instruction changes how the model responds. It does not turn the output into verified expert advice.

questions.question: Which instruction helps prevent invented details in a draft?
options: Use only supplied information and mark what is missing
Infer typical observations where the transcript is incomplete
Use a polished narrative without missing-data markers
Make uncertain details sound like established observations
questions.explanation: Clear constraints reduce unsupported additions, but checking is still required.

questions.question: What is the first step in the notes' documentation workflow?
options: De-identify a recording obtained without prior consent
Generate a SOAP draft before reviewing recording permissions
Record or transcribe with consent using an approved tool
Sign the draft before comparing it with the transcript
questions.explanation: Consent and an approved process precede AI-assisted drafting.

questions.question: What should happen to a transcript before it is supplied to an LLM?
options: Remove only the client's first name and retain all other identifiers
Insert a likely diagnosis to improve the model's context
Merge prompted and independent successes to simplify the input
De-identify it
questions.explanation: De-identification reduces exposure of identifying information.

questions.question: How should missing information be handled in a SOAP draft?
options: Infer the most likely value from similar patients
Treat an omitted detail as a normal finding
Use a typical value without labeling it as an assumption
Mark it as [NOT STATED]
questions.explanation: A missing detail should remain visibly missing. Do not turn a guess into a recorded fact.

questions.question: What should happen before a clinician signs an AI-assisted note?
options: Check grammar and formatting without checking facts
Accept the note if it has all four SOAP headings
Ask the model to confirm its own accuracy
Check and correct it against the transcript and observations
questions.explanation: The clinician remains responsible for the final signed record.

questions.question: Which description best fits the LLM's documentation role?
options: A drafting scribe under clinician review
The treating clinician
The owner of the care plan
The final diagnostic authority
questions.explanation: The notes explicitly place clinical responsibility with the clinician.

questions.question: What belongs in Subjective?
options: Measurable trial counts and prompt levels
Clinical interpretation of progress
Client or caregiver report
Next goals and home-practice frequency
questions.explanation: This is what the client or caregiver reports. Make clear who supplied the information and do not invent it.

questions.question: What belongs in Objective?
options: Caregiver descriptions of behavior at home
The clinician's interpretation of progress
Planned treatment frequency and future targets
Measurable trials, accuracy and prompt levels
questions.explanation: This is what was measured or observed, such as trial counts and prompt levels. Keep it tied to actual session data.

questions.question: What belongs in Assessment?
options: The caregiver's reported concerns
Raw counts with no interpretation
Clinical interpretation of progress
The next appointment schedule alone
questions.explanation: This explains what the results mean for progress. The clinician must write or approve this interpretation.

questions.question: What belongs in Plan?
options: Only the client's report of the previous week
Next goals, frequency and home practice
Only the measured success rate from the session
Only the interpretation of the present results
questions.explanation: This describes what happens next, such as goals, session frequency and home practice. The clinician approves the plan.

questions.question: Which section should contain 'caregiver reports difficulty practicing at home'?
options: Objective
Assessment
Plan
Subjective
questions.explanation: This is reported experience rather than a counted performance measure.

questions.question: Which section should contain 'two independent correct responses in six trials'?
options: Subjective
Objective
Assessment
Plan
questions.explanation: Trial counts are measurable session data.

questions.question: What does I+ mean in the notes' coding scheme?
options: Correct after prompting
No response
Correct independently
Incorrect response
questions.explanation: I+ distinguishes independent success from supported success.

questions.question: What does P+ mean?
options: Correct after a prompt
A final diagnosis
No response
Correct independently
questions.explanation: P+ records successful performance with support.

questions.question: What does NR mean?
options: Not recorded as an independent success
No response
Not reviewed by the clinician
Normal response accuracy
questions.explanation: NR is a trial outcome and remains part of the trial total in the examples.

questions.question: With 2 I+, 2 P+, 1 incorrect and 1 NR, what is independent accuracy?
options: 2/4, exactly 50%
4/6, approximately 67%
2/6, approximately 33%
6/6, exactly 100%
questions.explanation: Only the two I+ responses were independent. Divide 2 by all 6 trials: about 33%.

questions.question: A six-trial record has 2 I+, 2 P+, 1 incorrect and 1 NR. What is accuracy with support?
options: 2/6, approximately 33%
4/6, approximately 67%
2/4, exactly 50%
1/6, approximately 17%
questions.explanation: Two independent and two prompted responses were correct. Divide all 4 correct responses by 6 trials: about 67%.

questions.question: A six-trial record has 2 I+, 2 P+, 1 incorrect and 1 NR. What is prompt dependence?
options: 2/4, exactly 50%
4/6, approximately 67%
1/6, approximately 17%
2/6, approximately 33%
questions.explanation: Two of the four successful responses needed a prompt. Divide 2 by 4: prompt dependence is 50%.

questions.question: A six-trial record has 2 I+, 2 P+, 1 incorrect and 1 NR. Why is 67% not its independent accuracy?
options: It uses all trials rather than only correct trials as the denominator
It combines prompted and independent successes
It excludes prompted successes from every measure
It treats no-response trials as independent successes
questions.explanation: Supported performance should not be presented as independent skill.

questions.question: The AI writes 'the child was cooperative,' but the transcript does not say this. What should happen?
options: Keep it if this is usual wording in the clinic's notes
Infer it from the absence of a reported problem
Remove it or mark it [NOT STATED]
Move it to Subjective without identifying a source
questions.explanation: Documentation must not turn plausible assumptions into reported observations.

questions.question: What should happen to unapproved diagnostic or prognostic statements in an AI draft?
options: Keep them if the model's explanation is persuasive
Delete or rewrite them under clinician judgment
Move them into Objective to avoid interpretation
Accept them when they match a common clinical pattern
questions.explanation: Interpretation and clinical judgments belong to the clinician.

questions.question: Who organized the 1956 Dartmouth AI workshop?
options: David Cope
Mikhail Bongard
John McCarthy
Andrej Karpathy
questions.explanation: McCarthy organized the workshop and introduced the name artificial intelligence.

questions.question: What is a 'suitcase word' in the book's discussion?
options: A technical term with one universally agreed definition
A term that refers only to a single measured score
A term containing many different meanings
A symbol that a computer cannot process
questions.explanation: The same word can carry several different meanings. The book calls intelligence a suitcase word because it includes many different abilities.

questions.question: What distinguishes the scientific aim of AI from its practical aim?
options: Replacing data versus creating sensors
Writing code versus avoiding computers
Understanding intelligence versus producing useful task performance
Selling hardware versus printing books
questions.explanation: The book distinguishes studying intelligence from building systems that perform well.

questions.question: Where does deep learning fit in the book's hierarchy?
options: AI is a subset of deep learning
Machine learning excludes AI
Within machine learning, which is within AI
Deep learning is identical to all AI
questions.explanation: Deep learning is one approach in a broader field.

questions.question: Who created the General Problem Solver?
options: LeCun and Hinton
Cope and Kurzweil
Allen Newell and Herbert Simon
Hubel and Wiesel
questions.explanation: GPS exemplified explicit symbolic representations and rules.

questions.question: In GPS, what does an operator do?
options: Evaluates only the final goal without changing states
Learns numerical weights from labeled images
Transforms the current problem state
Maps a problem directly to a memorized solution
questions.explanation: Operators change states subject to the problem's constraints.

questions.question: Why could GPS replace a meaningful symbol with a nonsense string and still work?
options: It understands river travel like a person
It manipulates formal relations rather than human meanings
It automatically learns every new language
It recognizes the string's emotional significance
questions.explanation: The program follows rules about how symbols relate. It does not need the human meaning of each word to perform the encoded operations.

questions.question: Who invented the perceptron?
options: Douglas Lenat
Terry Winograd
Seymour Papert
Frank Rosenblatt
questions.explanation: Rosenblatt developed this influential brain-inspired learning model.

questions.question: Where does a perceptron's learned knowledge reside?
options: Only a manually written collection of if-then rules
Only the raw examples stored unchanged
Only the final output label after prediction
Its weights and threshold
questions.explanation: Training changes numerical values governing its output.

questions.question: An 18 by 18 pixel image supplies how many pixel inputs in the book's example?
questions.explanation: The number of pixels is 18 multiplied by 18.

questions.question: What was an important limitation of simple perceptrons discussed by Minsky and Papert?
options: They required no training
Only a restricted class of problems could be solved perfectly
They understood every perceptual task
They could not add numerical inputs
questions.explanation: The book distinguishes limitations of simple perceptrons from the potential of multilayer networks.

questions.question: What is an AI winter?
options: A scheduled phase in every network training epoch
A period of reduced support after expectations are disappointed
A period when symbolic AI was proved universally correct
A temporary reduction in model error during training
questions.explanation: Cycles of optimism and overpromising have been followed by reduced funding and activity.

questions.question: What does 'easy things are hard' highlight?
options: AI difficulty always matches the difficulty humans experience
Expert-level chess necessarily requires everyday common sense
Everyday human abilities can be difficult for AI
A fast numerical calculation requires broad human understanding
questions.explanation: Vision, ordinary language and flexible learning proved harder than early researchers expected.

questions.question: What is a hidden unit?
options: A correct label held back during testing
A final category output not displayed to users
A human-specified network hyperparameter
A unit between input and output processing
questions.explanation: A hidden unit helps process information between the input and the final output. Hidden does not mean it performs no calculation.

questions.question: What can intermediate neural layers learn?
options: Only copies of the target labels
Only a fixed rule supplied for each category
More abstract features than raw inputs
Only the same representation repeated unchanged
questions.explanation: The book illustrates combining simpler features into useful representations.

questions.question: What does back-propagation address?
options: How to select a complete architecture without human decisions
How to establish external clinical validity automatically
How to assign output error to network weights
How to assign a label without comparing predictions with targets
questions.explanation: When the final answer is wrong, back-propagation helps determine which weights to adjust. It spreads error information backward through the network.

questions.question: How does neural-network learning occur in this account?
options: Repeatedly changing labels to agree with the current prediction
Gradual changes to connection weights
Adding a new explicit rule for every example
Changing only the reported confidence after training
questions.explanation: The learned numerical parameters determine how inputs map to outputs.

questions.question: What did the book's digit-recognition comparison illustrate?
options: No model needed training data
The perceptron always achieved perfect accuracy
A network with hidden units outperformed the simple perceptron
Hidden units made classification impossible
questions.explanation: The example reported approximately 94% for the network versus 80% for the perceptron.

questions.question: Which tasks can neural networks address besides image recognition?
options: Only handwritten digits
Only hardware assembly
Only logic puzzles
Speech recognition, translation and music tasks
questions.explanation: Neural networks can process different types of numerical representations.

questions.question: What does 'connectionism' emphasize?
options: Knowledge stored exclusively in readable logical rules
Knowledge distributed through weighted connections
Knowledge stored as a separate fact for every example
Knowledge derived entirely from a fixed search tree
questions.explanation: The model’s knowledge is spread across weighted connections. It is not stored only as separate readable rules.

questions.question: Which work is associated with Rumelhart and McClelland?
options: The Winograd schemas
The Dartmouth funding proposal
The ImageNet label list
Parallel Distributed Processing
questions.explanation: Their 1986 work became a major statement of connectionism.

questions.question: Why were expert systems limited beyond narrow domains?
options: Experts could state every relevant assumption explicitly
The systems automatically learned open-ended common sense
Adding more rules removed every representational limitation
Much expert knowledge is tacit and difficult to encode
questions.explanation: Explicit rules struggled to capture the background knowledge experts use.

questions.question: What made MYCIN a symbolic AI example?
options: Learning blood-disease categories from unlabeled recordings
Predicting medical text with a generative network
Expert-derived rules and explainable inference
Updating a Q-table through simulated treatment rewards
questions.explanation: MYCIN used rules elicited from physicians along with reasoning methods.

questions.question: What does GOFAI refer to?
options: General online feature aggregation
Good old-fashioned AI
Generative output for artificial images
Global object-free adaptive inference
questions.explanation: The term was used for symbolic AI approaches.

questions.question: Which developments helped enable the later machine-learning revival?
options: The disappearance of the internet
More data and computing power
Universal agreement on intelligence
An end to numerical processing
questions.explanation: More examples and faster computers made larger learning systems practical. Earlier systems were limited by both.

questions.question: In the book, what is narrow AI?
options: Any system with low accuracy
Any system with fewer than ten input variables
A system for one task or a small related task set
A system capable of integrating skills across arbitrary domains
questions.explanation: Narrow describes the scope of competence rather than the quality of performance.

questions.question: Why does a collection of narrow skills not automatically establish general intelligence?
options: General intelligence requires integration and flexible use
Each additional narrow skill automatically improves all others
General intelligence depends only on the number of trained models
Integrating abilities requires only increasing computer speed
questions.explanation: Being good at separate tasks is different from combining skills flexibly. General intelligence concerns that broader ability to adapt.

questions.question: What does anthropomorphism mean in discussions of AI?
options: Attributing human qualities to machines
Comparing systems using a shared benchmark
Measuring a model against a held-out dataset
Explaining a symbolic inference through its rules
questions.explanation: This means describing a machine as if it had human qualities. Words like understands can suggest more than the evidence shows.

questions.question: How did Searle use 'strong AI'?
options: The claim that a suitably programmed computer literally has a mind
Only a program with high classification accuracy
Any successful speech recognizer
Any system that runs quickly
questions.explanation: Searle's usage differs from the common narrow-versus-general distinction.

questions.question: What did Searle's 'weak AI' view allow?
options: No useful role for computers
Only computers made from biological cells
Proof that every chatbot has consciousness
Computers as tools for simulating intelligence
questions.explanation: This terminology concerns claims about having a mind.

questions.question: What is the Turing test's central setup?
options: Testing only whether the machine has a biological brain
Comparing image labels on a fixed benchmark
Requiring a machine to explain every internal weight
A judge distinguishes a human from a computer through conversation
questions.explanation: The imitation game evaluates behavior through an exchange rather than inspecting physical material.

questions.question: Why does test design matter in interpreting Turing-test claims?
options: Every conversation has an identical difficulty
A single fooled judge proves consciousness
The physical keyboard determines intelligence
Judge expertise, duration and rules affect the outcome
questions.explanation: A brief conversation with an inexperienced judge is a different test from a long expert interview. Test conditions affect what a result means.

questions.question: Why did the book question the Eugene Goostman publicity?
options: It was an image classifier
Conversational tricks and contest conditions weakened the intelligence claim
The test contained only arithmetic
The system had no text interface
questions.explanation: A narrow success at fooling judges does not settle broad questions about intelligence.

questions.question: What is an intelligence explosion in the discussion?
options: A proposed cycle in which smarter systems improve intelligence further
A guaranteed increase in understanding from more processor speed
A fixed set of unrelated narrow abilities
A benchmark improvement caused only by new test labels
questions.explanation: The chapter presents this as a speculative idea associated with I. J. Good.

questions.question: What kind of growth underpins Kurzweil's predictions discussed in the book?
options: Guaranteed linear growth in wisdom
A decline in all data sources
Exponential technological growth
No change in computing capacity
questions.explanation: The rice-doubling example explains the intuition behind exponential trends.

questions.question: What does reverse engineering the brain mean here?
options: Copying a person's name into a prompt
Understanding principles well enough to reproduce relevant functions
Making a computer case resemble a head
Counting the keys on a computer
questions.explanation: The idea concerns mechanisms and principles, not physical appearance alone.

questions.question: How should the book's dated forecasts about general AI be read?
options: As verified present-day facts
As historical predictions and debated views
As clinical instructions
As proof that all experts agree
questions.explanation: The chapter records competing expectations, rather than a settled timeline.

questions.question: What does the soldier-and-dog photograph illustrate?
options: Correct object labels establish a complete understanding of an event
Scene context can be inferred from pixel values without prior knowledge
Scene understanding extends beyond naming objects
Every plausible interpretation of a photograph is equally supported
questions.explanation: People combine visual information with background knowledge and plausible context.

questions.question: Why was the 1966 Summer Vision Project overoptimistic?
options: Images contained no numerical information
Describing visual scenes proved much harder than expected
No one could connect a camera
All objects looked identical
questions.explanation: The project underestimated the complexity of ordinary visual understanding.

questions.question: What is object recognition?
options: Describing the intentions of every visible person
Locating only the exact boundary of each object
Assigning an object category to visual information
Predicting all future events in a visual scene
questions.explanation: Recognition links patterns in pixels with categories such as dog or balloon.

questions.question: Why is recognizing dogs across images difficult?
options: Appearance changes with viewpoint, lighting, occlusion and breed
All images have the same scale
Every dog has identical pixel values
Image backgrounds are always blank
questions.explanation: A useful recognizer must tolerate substantial variation.

questions.question: What are invariant features intended to support?
options: Sensitivity to the exact training viewpoint only
Memorization of the background for each category
Recognition despite changes in appearance
Dependence on the image's original scale and lighting
questions.explanation: Earlier vision systems sought stable cues across different depictions.

questions.question: Whose visual-cortex findings helped inspire hierarchical vision networks?
options: Kurzweil and Kapor
Newell and Simon
Cope and Sims
Hubel and Wiesel
questions.explanation: Their work described responses to features of increasing complexity.

questions.question: Which model preceded and inspired ConvNets?
options: Copycat's letter strings
Fukushima's neocognitron
Cyc's logical assertions
Watson's Jeopardy buzzer
questions.explanation: The neocognitron influenced later convolutional-network designs.

questions.question: What does a receptive field describe?
options: The collection of all output categories
The complete training set for a layer
The interval between two weight updates
The input region to which a unit responds
questions.explanation: A unit looks at a particular part of its input. That area is its receptive field.

questions.question: What is shared within a basic ConvNet activation map?
options: Different independent weights for every location
The final classification label across every image
The feature-detecting weights across locations
An identical activation value at all spatial positions
questions.explanation: The same detector is used at several locations. Shared weights let it look for a feature wherever it appears.

questions.question: What does a convolutional hierarchy tend to combine?
options: High-level labels directly into raw pixels during every forward pass
Only identical features without any transformation
A complete symbolic description supplied by a human
Simple features into increasingly complex patterns
questions.explanation: Higher layers can combine lower-level feature responses.

questions.question: What supplies the classification module in the illustrated ConvNet?
options: Only the human-written category names
Only the raw training labels
The highest convolutional layer's activation maps
Only a list of detector definitions written by the programmer
questions.explanation: The classification stage uses the learned high-level visual representation.

questions.question: What is an epoch of training?
options: A single update after one training example
A full independent test of every possible image
One pass through the training examples
The final confidence score for one category
questions.explanation: Training usually involves repeated epochs with weight updates.

questions.question: Which early ConvNet is associated with Yann LeCun?
options: EMI
LeNet
Cyc
Metacat
questions.explanation: LeNet combined convolutional ideas with learning through back-propagation.

questions.question: What is a benchmark dataset?
options: A dataset proving that a model works in all populations
A dataset that must be included in training and final testing
A collection containing every rare real-world situation
A shared dataset used to compare methods
questions.explanation: Benchmarks standardize a task and evaluation, within their own limits.

questions.question: What resource supplied ImageNet's conceptual organization?
options: A Q-table
A SOAP template
A single handwritten alphabet
WordNet
questions.explanation: Fei-Fei Li linked many images to nouns organized through WordNet.

questions.question: Why were human annotators important to ImageNet?
options: Annotators supplied all network weights manually
Search results needed reliable labels
Annotators made independent testing unnecessary
Annotators wrote a complete rule for recognizing each object
questions.explanation: Large-scale labeled data depended on substantial human work.

questions.question: Which service supported large-scale ImageNet labeling?
options: A hospital billing system
A robot soccer league
IBM's Jeopardy buzzer
Amazon Mechanical Turk
questions.explanation: The service connected labeling tasks with human workers.

questions.question: What does top-5 accuracy count as correct?
options: The correct label appears among five proposed categories
The correct label is the first proposed category only
All five proposed labels must be present in the image
Five separate test images must be labeled correctly
questions.explanation: The answer counts as correct if the right category is anywhere in the five guesses. That is easier than requiring the first guess to be right.

questions.question: Which network won the influential 2012 ImageNet competition?
options: Copycat
AlexNet
Cyc
MYCIN
questions.explanation: AlexNet's result helped renew broad interest in deep convolutional networks.

questions.question: Which combination was central to the ConvNet breakthrough described in the book?
options: Large labeled datasets and fast parallel hardware
Only a smaller display
No data and no computation
Only a new definition of consciousness
questions.explanation: Scaling earlier ideas became feasible with data and computing advances.

questions.question: What is data snooping in the evaluation example?
options: Holding test labels away from model development
Using separate training and test examples
Using test feedback to guide model changes
Reporting the chosen hyperparameters before evaluation
questions.explanation: Using test results to keep improving the model lets the test influence development. The final score then becomes a less fair measure of new performance.

questions.question: Why should 'better than humans at vision' headlines be questioned?
options: A benchmark contains all real-world cases
Human vision is identical to top-5 labeling
Computer output can never be useful
A narrow benchmark result does not establish general visual ability
questions.explanation: The chapter separates ImageNet classification from broader visual understanding.

questions.question: What caveat applied to the human ImageNet comparison discussed in the book?
options: No human had access to images
Every human in the world took the test
Humans were allowed unlimited written descriptions
The often-cited human error figure came from one trained evaluator
questions.explanation: The design of a human comparison affects what can reasonably be claimed.

questions.question: How does localization differ from classification?
options: It assigns only a category without any spatial information
It measures the top-five confidence values
It identifies whether the training set is sufficiently large
It identifies where an object is, rather than only naming its category
questions.explanation: A correct category does not show that the model relied on the correct image region.

questions.question: Which is a hyperparameter rather than an ordinarily learned weight?
options: The chosen learning rate
A patient's recorded utterance
A connection value updated during training
A computed output activation
questions.explanation: Humans configure aspects of learning such as learning rate and architecture.

questions.question: Why is 'the network taught itself' an incomplete description?
options: All network structure is discovered without design choices
Humans design architecture, data and learning settings
Every training label is generated by the network itself
Back-propagation sets all hyperparameters independently
questions.explanation: Learning takes place within a substantial human-designed framework.

questions.question: What does the long-tail problem describe?
options: A small set of common cases with many examples each
A large increase in accuracy on the training set
Many rare but possible situations with little training coverage
An unusually deep final hidden layer
questions.explanation: There can be many unusual events, even if each is rare. A model may have seen few or no examples of these events during training.

questions.question: Why is labeling every possible driving scenario impractical?
options: Real-world situations are open-ended and numerous
Cars encounter only traffic lights
Labels are never used in vision
Every road scene is identical
questions.explanation: A finite supervised dataset cannot anticipate all unusual situations.

questions.question: What shortcut did the animal-classifier example learn?
options: The causal biological features shared by all animals
Only the exact outline of each animal species
A complete representation of animal behavior
Background blur associated with animal photographs
questions.explanation: Animal photographs often had blurred backgrounds. The model used that accidental clue instead of reliably recognizing the animal itself.

questions.question: Why might a shortcut model perform well on an ordinary test set?
options: The test data share the same accidental correlation
The model is necessarily unbiased
It contains no relevant pixels
The test set proves causal understanding
questions.explanation: A shared dataset artifact can make a shortcut look like successful learning.

questions.question: What is overfitting in the chapter's discussion?
options: Successful transfer across unrelated tasks
A deliberate attempt to fool a model with a targeted input
Choosing the number of layers before training
Learning patterns that do not transfer robustly beyond the data
questions.explanation: The model fits its examples too narrowly. It may score well on familiar data but struggle when relevant conditions change.

questions.question: What can an unrepresentative face dataset produce?
options: Automatic fairness across all populations
Perfect recognition for every face
No effect on predictions
Unequal recognition error rates across groups
questions.explanation: Representation in training data influences performance and potential harms.

questions.question: What is the aim of interpretable machine learning?
options: Increasing accuracy without considering explanations
Making model decisions understandable to humans
Producing a persuasive narrative regardless of its relation to the decision
Replacing subgroup evaluation with one overall score
questions.explanation: Interpretability seeks insight into what drives a decision.

questions.question: What is an adversarial example?
options: Any input that produces a naturally occurring error
Any test image not included in training
An input deliberately altered to induce a model error
Any low-confidence prediction on a valid example
questions.explanation: Someone deliberately changes an input to trick the model. A tiny change can sometimes produce a very confident wrong answer.

questions.question: What do high-confidence errors demonstrate?
options: Confidence is not a guarantee of correctness
Only low-confidence outputs require checking
Confidence proves humanlike understanding
All confident outputs are malicious
questions.explanation: Models can strongly prefer a wrong category, including on adversarial inputs.

questions.question: What does Clever Hans symbolize in machine learning?
options: Learning an abstract rule that transfers to every context
Apparent understanding based on unintended cues
Solving a task through an independently verified explanation
Reaching high accuracy without using any training information
questions.explanation: The horse appeared to understand arithmetic but followed subtle human cues. The lesson is that a correct answer can come from an unintended shortcut.

questions.question: Which is a potential benefit of AI discussed in the chapter?
options: Perfect fairness without evaluation
Removal of every ethical dilemma
Helping analyze scientific data and support accessibility
Guaranteed elimination of every illness
questions.explanation: The chapter balances useful applications with risks and limits.

questions.question: Why does the electricity analogy have limits in the book?
options: Electricity was never commercialized
Electricity cannot be useful
AI behavior is less well understood and predictable
AI needs no energy
questions.explanation: The author questions deployment before capabilities and failures are adequately understood.

questions.question: Why is facial recognition ethically complex?
options: It has no useful applications
It affects only image storage costs
It can aid identification while threatening privacy and civil rights
It can never make mistakes
questions.explanation: The same capability can support beneficial and harmful uses.

questions.question: What did the ACLU example illustrate in the chapter?
options: Congress members supplied criminal labels
False matches and disproportionate errors can have social consequences
A correct match removes all privacy concerns
Every match is a confirmed identity
questions.explanation: The example concerns both reliability and the distribution of errors.

questions.question: Why are AI governance issues more than technical problems?
options: Model architecture alone determines acceptable use
Only programmers can be affected
All ethical decisions have one agreed mathematical answer
They involve social values, rights and political decisions
questions.explanation: Questions of responsibility and acceptable use require broader participation.

questions.question: What regulatory analogy does Mitchell favor in this discussion?
options: Cooperation resembling biological and medical technology oversight
Removing every quality-assurance step
Letting advertising alone regulate use
Allowing only vendors to assess themselves
questions.explanation: The author proposes shared oversight involving multiple institutions.

questions.question: Why are Asimov's robot laws not a complete engineering solution?
options: They specify every real-world situation
Rules can conflict and produce unintended consequences
They are a verified software standard
They remove ambiguity from morality
questions.explanation: The stories themselves explored failures arising from simple moral rules.

questions.question: What is the value alignment problem?
options: Ensuring every user prefers the same outcome
Ensuring a model maximizes a numerical objective regardless of consequences
Making all systems report identical confidence scores
Ensuring system aims match the human purposes actually intended
questions.explanation: The system should pursue the goal people actually intend. Maximizing a convenient score can be harmful if that score captures the wrong goal.

questions.question: What does the trolley problem explore?
options: A forced choice between harmful outcomes
A method for estimating the best action value from rewards
A test that determines one universally accepted moral rule
A way to eliminate uncertainty from real-world driving
questions.explanation: The thought experiment highlights ethical trade-offs, but is highly simplified.

questions.question: What inconsistency appeared in the autonomous-vehicle survey?
options: People endorsed self-sacrifice in principle but preferred self-protection for their own car
Everyone chose the same car for the same reason
Everyone rejected pedestrian safety
No one expressed a moral preference
questions.explanation: Stated collective values can conflict with personal purchasing preferences.

questions.question: Why is learning moral values from human behavior problematic?
options: Learning removes every governance concern
All observed behavior is morally ideal
Human behavior can be biased, inconsistent and difficult to interpret
Rewards always encode every value correctly
questions.explanation: Learning ethics inherits the limitations of data-driven learning.

questions.question: Which response best reflects the chapter's overall approach to AI benefits and risks?
options: Assume every new system is safe
Treat market success as ethical proof
Ban every computational tool
Assess both usefulness and possible harm before granting trust
questions.explanation: Useful technology still requires assessment of reliability, fairness and use.

questions.question: What psychological idea inspired reinforcement learning in the example?
options: Classical symbolic deduction
Distributional semantics
Operant conditioning
Supervised category labeling
questions.explanation: Consequences can shape behavior through rewards.

questions.question: What feedback does pure reinforcement learning use?
options: Only a written rule for every situation
Rewards from actions
A correct category label for every input
An expert's full reasoning transcript
questions.explanation: Rewards may arrive intermittently rather than after every useful action.

questions.question: In reinforcement learning, what is a state?
options: The reward received after the next action
The complete list of actions available to the designer
The agent's representation of its current situation
The rule used to update all model parameters
questions.explanation: The Rosie example simplifies state to estimated distance from the ball.

questions.question: Which actions are available to Rosie in the simplified example?
options: Translate, diagnose and summarize
Forward, backward and kick
Classify, consent and bill
Read, write and sign
questions.explanation: A small action space makes the learning example manageable.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an action value?
options: To report only the immediate reward already received
To indicate how often an action was named in a rule set
To predict future reward associated with an action in a state
To describe the agent's current sensor reading without future consequences
questions.explanation: An action can be useful because it helps reach a later reward. Its value is not limited to what it earns immediately.

questions.question: What does a Q-table store?
options: The entire chronological history of every observation
One fixed reward for each action regardless of state
The hidden activations of a trained word encoder
Values for state-action combinations
questions.explanation: For each situation and possible action, the table stores an estimated value. Experience updates those estimates.

questions.question: Why can delayed reward make learning difficult?
options: The agent sees a correct label for every step
All actions are equally useful
The agent must assign credit to earlier actions
Only the final action ever matters
questions.explanation: Earlier actions may enable later rewards without receiving immediate feedback.

questions.question: Why are future rewards discounted in the example?
options: To make every action identical
To favor efficient paths to actual reward
To erase all rewards
To prevent any learning
questions.explanation: The example reduces values as reward is propagated backward in time.

questions.question: What is exploration?
options: Always choosing the current highest-value action
Reducing the reward discount to zero
Trying actions whose value is not yet well known
Stopping after the first successful episode
questions.explanation: Try an option you do not yet know much about. It might lead to a better outcome than your current favorite.

questions.question: What is exploitation?
options: Trying only actions that have never been attempted
Selecting each action with equal probability indefinitely
Changing the reward definition after each failed episode
Choosing actions with known high estimated value
questions.explanation: Use the option that experience currently suggests is good. Good learning balances this with trying alternatives.

questions.question: Why is a Q-table impractical for complex driving?
options: Driving has no sensor inputs
Tables cannot contain numbers
The possible states are far too numerous
Cars have only one possible state
questions.explanation: Rich continuous observations make enumerating all states infeasible.

questions.question: What is a major limitation of simulation-based training?
options: Learned behavior may not transfer to the unpredictable real world
Real robots never need evaluation
Simulation guarantees real-world safety
Every simulation contains all events
questions.explanation: The simulation-to-reality gap grows with environmental complexity.

questions.question: Why are games attractive research environments for AI?
options: Their outcomes cannot be measured
They require no computation
They provide controlled rules, actions and feedback
They contain every feature of the real world
questions.explanation: Games provide useful constrained testbeds.

questions.question: What combines deep networks with Q-learning?
options: A symbolic rule-based expert system
A recurrent word-embedding model
Deep Q-learning
A Monte Carlo search method without a learned network
questions.explanation: A neural network estimates action values instead of storing a separate table entry for every situation. This helps with much larger inputs.

questions.question: Why did the Atari DQN use several successive frames?
options: To include limited information about recent motion
To supply human labels for every possible action
To reveal all future rewards directly
To replace the need for learning action values
questions.explanation: Multiple frames provide a small amount of memory.

questions.question: What did DQN outputs estimate?
options: The exact human label of each visible object
Values for possible actions
Only the immediate reward already received
The probability that a sentence has positive sentiment
questions.explanation: The network links the current state representation with action-value estimates.

questions.question: What is temporal-difference learning concerned with?
options: Deleting all past experience
Comparing two computer clocks only
Labeling every frame with a diagnosis
Updating predictions using differences across successive estimates and rewards
