questions.explanation: A prediction of future reward is updated using later information and rewards. Learning comes from the difference between estimates over time.

questions.question: Did DeepMind's original Atari work transfer the learned weights from one game to the next?
options: Yes, every game used one already-trained player
Yes, without further learning
No, each game was learned separately
No games required training

questions.question: What notable behavior emerged in the Breakout example?
options: Creating a tunnel to reach high-value bricks from above
Recognizing all real-world tunnels
Reading a written strategy manual
Refusing every reward

questions.question: Who is associated with the early checkers-learning program?
options: Arthur Samuel
David Cope
Mikhail Bongard
Terry Winograd

questions.question: What does a game-tree evaluation function estimate?
options: How favorable a board position is
Only the number of legal moves already made
The opponent's actual emotional response
The exact outcome of every possible full game

Selecting moves by propagating position evaluations through a partial tree
Learning a word representation from context pairs
Updating every weight using labeled image errors

questions.question: What distinguishes Deep Blue from AlphaGo in this account?

Deep Blue relied heavily on search and engineered evaluation rather than central machine learning
AlphaGo used no learned networks
Deep Blue could play every game

questions.question: How did AlphaGo Zero differ from its predecessor in initial game examples?
options: It had no rules or human-designed architecture

It needed no training games
It used only an expert's move list

questions.question: What does Monte Carlo tree search use to evaluate possibilities?
options: Statistics from simulated continuations
Exhaustive enumeration of every possible full game
Only a fixed human evaluation score with no simulation
Only the frequency of moves in an expert's written rules
questions.explanation: The search tries simulated continuations and collects results. Those results help compare promising moves.

questions.question: What is transfer learning in the chapter's broad discussion?
options: Training the same architecture independently on each task
Copying an unchanged training set into the test set
Applying learned knowledge to a different task or situation
Increasing training epochs on the identical examples
questions.explanation: Use something already learned to help with a different task or situation. Starting again from scratch is not the same kind of transfer.

questions.question: Why is using the same architecture for chess and Go not sufficient evidence of transfer?
options: Shared architecture guarantees shared concepts
Different networks can still learn each game from scratch
The games have identical rules
Architecture is always a learned weight

questions.question: What human contributions remained important in AlphaGo Zero?
options: Only choosing the program's name
None beyond observing play
Only switching on a monitor
Architecture, search method and hyperparameter choices
questions.explanation: The chapter challenges overly broad claims about learning without human guidance.

questions.question: What did simple algorithm comparisons on Atari caution against?
options: Assuming that impressive scores reveal uniquely deep intelligence
Evaluating more than one method
Reporting test conditions
Using baseline comparisons
questions.explanation: Strong simple baselines help establish what a complex method contributes.

questions.question: Why is charades a difficult AI challenge in Mitchell's discussion?
options: It has no human communication
It integrates social, visual and linguistic understanding
It uses only one fixed numeric action
It is simply identical to Go
questions.explanation: Difficulty for humans and difficulty for AI need not coincide.

questions.question: Why can saying the Breakout agent 'understands tunneling' mislead?
options: The behavior may not reflect a transferable concept
It proves mastery of underground construction
It guarantees all related skills
It describes a verified internal explanation

questions.question: What did sensitivity to small game changes suggest?
options: Perfect causal understanding
Guaranteed flexible reasoning
No dependence on the input
Limited generalization beyond training conditions

questions.question: Can deep reinforcement-learning systems also be vulnerable to adversarial inputs?
options: No, rewards prevent every attack
Yes, targeted input changes can disrupt performance
Only symbolic systems can be attacked
Only human players can be fooled

questions.question: Why does a chess-playing child illustrate a different kind of intelligence from AlphaGo?
options: The child can apply flexible thinking across activities
The child never makes errors
The child must always win at Go
The child calculates more positions per second
questions.explanation: Human intelligence involves broad adaptation beyond one mastered game.

questions.question: Why are game reward functions easier than many real-world objectives?
options: Real-world objectives always have clearer single rewards
Scores or wins are relatively clear and bounded
Every game includes the full complexity of physical interaction
A game's reward proves the agent understands human goals
questions.explanation: Real-world objectives can be ambiguous and competing.

questions.question: What challenge appears in defining a dishwasher robot's state?
options: Removing all sensory data
Deciding which objects and surrounding events are relevant
Reading an already complete game board
Knowing only the exact final reward

questions.question: What does the chapter treat game-playing success as?
options: A reason to stop studying transfer
Proof that healthcare deployment is automatically safe
Evidence that every AI problem is solved
A proof of principle with important limits on generalization

questions.question: What does the restaurant story show about language comprehension?
options: It requires background knowledge, reference and pragmatic interpretation
Sarcasm is always literal praise
Events need no causal interpretation
Only isolated word lookup is needed
questions.explanation: Understanding the story involves much more than transcribing words.

questions.question: What does automatic speech recognition do?
options: Interprets all intentions behind the speech
Assigns a clinical diagnosis to every speaker
Generates a translation into a different language by definition
Transforms speech into text
questions.explanation: ASR concerns transcription, which is different from understanding meaning.

questions.question: Why can background noise reduce recognition accuracy?
options: It supplies correct labels
It removes every ambiguity
It gives the system more verified context
It changes or obscures the acoustic input
questions.explanation: Recognition performance depends on recording conditions.

questions.question: Why are homophones challenging for ASR?
options: Their sound always uniquely identifies the spelling
Choosing the intended word can require context and world knowledge
They cannot occur in ordinary speech
They all mean the same thing
questions.explanation: The book uses mousse/moose and bare/bear examples.

questions.question: What is sentiment classification?
options: Assigning an opinion category such as positive or negative
Determining which word a spoken sound represents
Resolving which person a pronoun refers to
Generating a target-language sentence
questions.explanation: The task concerns expressed evaluation or attitude.

questions.question: Why is counting negative words insufficient for sentiment analysis?
options: Negation and context can change the meaning
All reviews have one sentence
Every negative word makes a review negative
Word order never matters
questions.explanation: A sentence can use negative-sounding words within an overall positive judgment.

questions.question: What distinguishes a recurrent neural network in the account?
options: Its current hidden state depends only on the present input
Each new word requires an entirely separate trained network
Its sequence representation never uses prior activations
Current processing also uses prior hidden activations
questions.explanation: The network uses information from earlier steps while processing the current word. That gives it some memory of the sequence.

questions.question: What is a network's vocabulary in the book's example?
options: Only the words seen in one current sentence
Every possible sentence the network can generate
The words it can accept as inputs
Only the category names used in final classification
questions.explanation: The input encoding is defined over a chosen vocabulary.

questions.question: What is one-hot encoding?
options: A vector with one active position for a word
A dense vector whose distances encode semantic similarity directly
A probability distribution across all possible sentences
A table of manually written definitions for every word
questions.explanation: Each word has its own position in a long vector. Only that position is active, so the code identifies the word without directly expressing its meaning.

questions.question: What is the distributional-semantics hypothesis?
options: Words with identical length always mean the same thing
Words in similar contexts tend to have related meanings
All word pairs are equally related
Meaning depends only on spelling
questions.explanation: Words used in similar surroundings often have related meanings. The approach learns from these patterns of use.

questions.question: What does word2vec learn?
options: Numerical vector representations from word contexts
A manually programmed taxonomy of all word meanings
A unique integer label with no learned contextual relationships
A complete symbolic description of every sentence
questions.explanation: The model learns a list of numbers for each word from its contexts. Related words can end up with related numerical patterns.

questions.question: Why can word vectors reproduce gender stereotypes?
options: Vectors are automatically fair
Geometry excludes social patterns
Only image datasets can be biased
They reflect biases in the language data used for training
questions.explanation: Language data can contain social stereotypes. A model that learns those patterns can carry the same stereotypes into later tasks.

questions.question: What training data supported statistical machine translation in the book?
options: Pairs of source sentences and human translations
Unpaired source-language words without target examples
Only dictionary definitions for each target word
Only the model's own unverified translations
questions.explanation: Parallel translated text supplies examples of cross-language correspondence.

questions.question: What is the encoder's role in the described translation model?
options: Generate the target sentence one word at a time
Compute only the BLEU score of a completed translation
Build a representation of the source sentence
Supply a manually written rule for every grammatical structure
questions.explanation: The encoder turns the source sentence into a representation the system can use. The decoder uses it to produce the translation.

questions.question: What is the decoder's role?
options: Generate the target-language sequence from the representation
Compress the source input before any output generation
Label every source word with a diagnosis
Rate a translation by counting reference overlaps
questions.explanation: The decoder creates the output sequence, such as a sentence in another language. It works from the representation provided by the encoder.

questions.question: Why did simple recurrent encoders struggle with long sentences?
options: The decoder could not output words
Long sentences contain no meaning
Every input word had the same vector
Important earlier information could be lost
questions.explanation: Compressing long dependencies into hidden states is challenging.

questions.question: What did LSTM units help manage?
options: The number of class labels in a vision benchmark
Only the vocabulary's alphabetical ordering
The threshold used to define a false positive
Retention and forgetting of information over time
questions.explanation: LSTM units help manage what information to keep and what to forget. This can help the model use earlier parts of a long sequence.

questions.question: What does BLEU primarily compare?
options: The percentage of patients correctly classified
The causal faithfulness of the translation model's internal explanation
Only the grammatical acceptability of a translation to one reader
Word and phrase overlap with reference translations
questions.explanation: BLEU counts matching words and phrases between a machine translation and human references. Matching wording is useful evidence, but not a complete test of meaning.

questions.question: Why is machine-translation evaluation difficult?
options: Human readers always agree perfectly
Several different translations can be valid
Every sentence has one exact acceptable wording
Translation has no measurable properties
questions.explanation: A reference translation is not the only possible good rendering.

questions.question: What can a good average translation rating conceal?
options: Perfect reliability in every case
Occasional serious failures
An absence of variation
Proof of full comprehension
questions.explanation: A high mean does not describe how severe or frequent bad outputs are.

questions.question: Why can sentence-by-sentence evaluation miss important errors?
options: Meaning may depend on relations across sentences
Every sentence is independent in real documents
Discourse never affects reference
Words have only one sense
questions.explanation: Document context may resolve references and ambiguities.

questions.question: What does the restaurant translation example demonstrate?
options: Dictionary substitution always works
All translations fail identically
Idioms and context can be mistranslated despite fluent output
Fluency guarantees faithful meaning
questions.explanation: Plausible wording can distort the intended events or meanings.

questions.question: How is image captioning framed in the chapter?
options: Matching an image to a fixed filename only
Translating a human-written caption into image pixels only
Encoding an image and decoding a description
Extracting an answer span from a supplied paragraph
questions.explanation: The source and target representations can differ in modality.

questions.question: Why are incorrect captions particularly concerning for blind users?
options: Users may be unable to check whether a description matches the image
Every caption can be independently seen by the user
A caption's grammar proves accuracy
Wrong captions contain no practical information
questions.explanation: Accessibility benefits depend on reliability, not only fluent descriptions.

questions.question: What did Watson combine to answer Jeopardy clues?

Multiple NLP, retrieval and scoring methods
Only a modern clinical chatbot prompt

It provided many labeled training examples
It guaranteed knowledge of every clinical case
It removed all need for evaluation

questions.question: Why does answering 'leg' differ from 'missing leg' in the Watson example?

The two phrases always mean the same thing
It misses the unusual condition the clue asks about
The clue concerns only spelling
questions.explanation: A related word can still fail to express the required meaning.

questions.question: Why did a Jeopardy victory not establish competence in medicine?

Every diagnosis is a short trivia response
Both domains always have identical data
Medical reasoning is only buzzer speed
questions.explanation: Task-specific success does not establish safe transfer to a new domain.

questions.question: What does the chapter warn about the Watson brand?
options: It proves all knowledge has been integrated

It guarantees a single general intelligence
It names only a keyboard
questions.explanation: Marketing language can blur distinctions among different tools and workflows.

questions.question: What did the original SQuAD benchmark require?

Resolve every implied event not mentioned in the passage
Translate the paragraph into a different language

questions.question: Why is answer extraction narrower than full reading comprehension?

It tests every kind of language use
It need not demonstrate broad inference or world understanding
It always requires more knowledge than any reading task
questions.explanation: Matching an answer span is useful but limited evidence of comprehension.

Only recognizing a named image
Only counting letters
Combining language with background knowledge and reasoning
questions.explanation: The science task challenged methods successful on answer-extraction benchmarks.

questions.question: What do Winograd schemas mainly test?
options: Recognizing whether two words have identical spelling

Resolving references using commonsense context
Measuring positive or negative sentiment
questions.explanation: These small puzzles ask which person or thing a pronoun refers to. Everyday knowledge often helps choose the answer.

questions.question: In 'I poured water from the bottle into the cup until it was full,' what is normally full?

The bottle
Neither container necessarily

questions.question: What can an irrelevant added sentence do to a vulnerable QA system?

Humans and recognizers always process sound identically

A limit on monitor resolution

questions.question: What is core knowledge in the chapter?

Only consciously stated rules acquired in adulthood
The model parameters learned from an image dataset

An occluded part remains part of the object
Only fully visible objects exist

Expectations about objects and causal interactions
A guarantee of perfect mathematical prediction

Other people's beliefs, goals and feelings
The set of allowable grammatical sentence structures
The fixed numerical threshold of a perceptron

A fixed category label assigned to a single object
A list of all words in the model vocabulary
A representation used to anticipate how a situation may unfold

Which exact past event must be repeated unchanged?
What might happen if circumstances were different?

questions.question: What does Barsalou's proposal connect with understanding?

Only arbitrary symbol lists
Only word frequency with no experience

questions.question: What is the Lakoff and Johnson view of everyday metaphor?
options: Every metaphor has one literal reading

Abstract ideas are often understood through concrete experience
Metaphor never affects thought

questions.question: What is abstraction?
options: Recognizing particular cases as instances of a more general pattern
Grouping only objects with identical surface appearances
Memorizing the full description of each separate example
Copying a category label without recognizing shared relations

Finding only identical words in two descriptions
Perceiving a common essence across things

As a complete scientific proof of consciousness

As explicitly speculative and theoretically unsettled

Explicitly encoded assertions and logical inference

Apply one predefined shape rule to every problem

A training dataset that includes all possible examples
An idealized domain for developing and testing ideas
questions.explanation: Microworlds simplify a problem but limit what success proves.

questions.question: What was Copycat designed to explore?

Learning motor actions from numeric rewards
Analogy-making with letter strings

Discarding all prior concepts before solving a problem

Perfect generalization to every analogy

questions.question: How does the author characterize predictions about AI replacing jobs?

options: Both always mean a final clinical diagnosis
Classification requires no data
Prediction estimates an outcome; classification assigns a category
Prediction is always true; classification is always false
questions.explanation: The terms describe computational output types, not guaranteed clinical truth.

questions.question: Which capability is especially important in human SLP practice?
options: Empathy and a therapeutic relationship
Accepting every prediction
Ignoring cultural context
Processing every dataset faster than a computer
questions.explanation: The deck highlights reasoning, interaction, empathy and shared decisions.

questions.question: What should happen after an AI produces a speech classification?
options: The software replaces the interview
The output is signed without review
The patient automatically receives a diagnosis
The SLP reviews whether it is clinically meaningful
questions.explanation: Prediction is followed by clinical interpretation.

questions.question: What does greater AI autonomy require according to the deck?
options: Fewer professional responsibilities
Stronger evidence and governance
No monitoring
Less validation
questions.explanation: Directly action-driving systems need especially strong justification and oversight.

questions.question: Which area is explicitly included in the deck's SLP scope?
options: Only retail marketing
Cognitive-communication and AAC
Only handwritten-number recognition
Only financial trading
questions.explanation: The deck lists speech, language, voice, fluency, swallowing and cognitive-communication/AAC.

questions.question: Which application concerns speech rather than text generation?
options: Drafting a caregiver leaflet
Acoustic analysis of recordings
Generating activity instructions
Writing a summary paragraph
questions.explanation: Speech AI can extract signal features and automated speech measures.

questions.question: Which application concerns language-sample analysis?
options: Examining vocabulary, syntax and semantic features
Counting only computer processors
Measuring screen size
Assigning a diagnosis from a person's name
questions.explanation: Language analysis can quantify aspects of structure and meaning.

questions.question: Which task is a reasonable generative-AI draft use listed in the deck?
options: Creating practice sentences for clinician review
Assigning eligibility without assessment
Guaranteeing a prognosis
Signing a report on behalf of the clinician
questions.explanation: The deck presents generation as support requiring verification.

questions.question: Why may an unusual patient be challenging for AI?
options: All models have seen every rare condition
The patient's patterns may differ from training examples
Rare cases require no context
The model's confidence eliminates uncertainty
questions.explanation: The deck highlights rare cases and generalization beyond training data as limits.

questions.question: Which question directly probes representativeness?
options: How many colors are in the logo?
What data was it trained on?
Does the answer use long words?
Is the interface animated?
questions.explanation: Training population details help assess whether evidence applies to a new patient.

questions.question: Which of the deck's five appraisal questions addresses failure consequences?
options: Which brand sounds more professional?
Can the answer be longer?
Is the model popular?
What could go wrong?
questions.explanation: Risks and error consequences belong in clinical appraisal.

questions.question: Which question protects professional accountability?
options: Where does the SLP remain responsible?
Can the model replace every clinician?
Can the report omit its reviewer?
Which software signs fastest?
questions.explanation: The deck keeps professional responsibility with the clinician.

questions.question: Which is a strength listed in the deck?
options: Guaranteed transfer to unseen populations
Repetitive analysis and processing large datasets
Reliable empathy in every interaction
Perfect cultural judgment
questions.explanation: AI can support high-volume computational tasks without possessing clinical judgment.

questions.question: Why is an AI-generated educational handout still checked?
options: Only numerical outputs can be wrong
All generated text is clinically validated
A role prompt guarantees factual accuracy
Fluent generated content can contain errors
questions.explanation: The deck's verification requirement applies to clinically relevant generated materials.

questions.question: Which is an example of a healthcare monitoring use?
options: Treating data collection as consent
Deleting all later observations
Assuming one output is a permanent diagnosis
Tracking changes in repeated measurements for clinician review
questions.explanation: Monitoring is among the healthcare functions listed in the deck.

questions.question: Of 100 children with a difficulty, a screener detects 90. What is sensitivity?
questions.explanation: Sensitivity is true positives divided by all genuinely affected cases: 90/100.

questions.question: Of 100 children without a difficulty, 76 are cleared. What is specificity?
questions.explanation: Specificity is true negatives divided by all genuinely unaffected cases: 76/100.

questions.question: A tool flags 40 children, of whom 30 truly have the difficulty. What is precision?
questions.explanation: Precision is true positives divided by all flagged cases: 30/40.

questions.question: A classifier is correct for 85 of 100 evaluated cases. What is accuracy?
questions.explanation: Accuracy uses all correct classifications over all evaluated cases.

questions.question: A screener misses 5 of 20 genuinely affected children. What is sensitivity?
questions.explanation: There are 15 true positives, so sensitivity is 15/20.

questions.question: A six-trial record contains 3 I+, 1 P+, 1 incorrect and 1 NR. What is independent accuracy?
questions.explanation: Independent accuracy is 3/6. Prompted successes are excluded from its numerator.

questions.question: For 3 I+, 1 P+, 1 incorrect and 1 NR, what is accuracy with support?
options: Approximately 67%
questions.explanation: All four correct responses are counted over six trials.

questions.question: For 3 I+, 1 P+, 1 incorrect and 1 NR, what is prompt dependence?
questions.explanation: Prompt dependence is 1/(3+1), which is 25%.

questions.question: A child has no correct responses. How should P+ divided by (I+ + P+) be handled?
options: Invent a correct response
Report it as undefined rather than divide by zero
Report 50% automatically
Report 100% automatically
questions.explanation: With no correct trials the denominator is zero, so that ratio cannot be calculated.

questions.question: A report gives overall accuracy but no language-group breakdown. What is the best next request?
options: A promise of perfect performance
A longer advertising description
Subgroup performance and relevant validation details
Only the model's logo
questions.explanation: Overall results may conceal poorer performance in a language group.

questions.question: An LLM combines 2 I+ and 2 P+ as four independent successes. What should the reviewer correct?
options: Remove every trial count
Keep the total as independent accuracy
Change the child's age
Separate independent from prompted responses and recalculate
questions.explanation: The mistake inflates independent skill by merging response categories.

questions.question: A generated note includes a client name that was missed during de-identification. What is the next step?
options: Add the client's address for consistency
Ignore it if the diagnosis is correct
Remove the identifier and follow the approved privacy process
Continue because only the final note matters
questions.explanation: Privacy checking includes identifiers in both inputs and drafts.

questions.question: A parent asks whether a positive AI screen proves DLD. What is the appropriate explanation?
options: It guarantees the same result in every language
It means therapy can be prescribed without review
It is a conclusive diagnosis
It indicates risk and needs full assessment
questions.explanation: The notes distinguish screening from diagnosis.

questions.question: An activity lists words lacking the requested initial /s/. What should happen?
options: Remove all instructions and keep the words
Accept it because the table is attractive
Correct the word list before use
Change the child's target to match the list
questions.explanation: Generated materials must be checked for the actual target sound and position.

questions.question: A user sets a paediatric SLP role but omits age, target and audience. What is the best improvement?
options: Use only more enthusiastic language
Add the client's complete medical record
Assume the model knows the case
Add de-identified context and precise output requirements
questions.explanation: Role alone does not communicate the relevant task details.

questions.question: Which support sequence is stated in the lecture notes?
options: Model, physical, verbal, independent, visual
Verbal, physical, independent, model, visual
Physical, independent, model, verbal, gestural
Independent, verbal, model, gestural/visual, physical
questions.explanation: This reproduces the hierarchy as presented in the supplied notes.

questions.question: What administrative benefit do the notes describe?
options: Eliminating all review duties
Removing consent requirements
Guaranteeing every assessment score
Reducing time spent drafting notes and reports
questions.explanation: Speech-to-text and summarization may reduce documentation burden when properly reviewed.

questions.question: What approximate publication growth rate is reported in the notes?
options: 100% per month
1% per decade
16.5% per year
0% per year
questions.explanation: This is the figure reported in the notes, not an independently updated literature estimate.

questions.question: What average waiting-list figure is cited in the notes?
options: Exactly one day
Around eight years
Around eight months
Exactly one week
questions.explanation: The notes use this reported figure to motivate early-access opportunities.

questions.question: What can multimodal data help identify for personalization?
options: A reason to ignore clinical history
A guaranteed universal treatment
The child's identity without consent
Which language subsystems drive a child's difficulty
questions.explanation: The notes connect different data sources with tailored targets and intensity.

questions.question: When six trials include no independent successes and three prompted successes, what is independent accuracy?
options: Undefined
questions.explanation: The denominator is six, so zero independent successes gives 0/6 rather than an undefined ratio.

questions.question: Which system defeated Garry Kasparov in 1997?
options: EMI
Metacat
IBM Deep Blue
Cyc
questions.explanation: The prologue uses computer chess to question assumptions about intelligence.

questions.question: Why did Deep Blue challenge Hofstadter's earlier expectation?
options: It showed that every computer had emotions
It learned every human language
Narrow chess mastery did not require broad general intelligence
It needed no specialized engineering
questions.explanation: The example separates success in chess from general humanlike ability.

questions.question: What surprised listeners in the EMI comparison described in the prologue?
options: They could mistake generated music for a human composer's work
Every listener identified every piece correctly
The program could not produce sound
The audience had no musical experience
questions.explanation: The incident raised questions about style imitation and perceived creativity.

questions.question: What particularly disturbed Hofstadter in the prologue?
options: The possibility that valued human creativity could be matched by superficial mechanisms
Only the length of music recordings
A proven inability of AI to generate anything
Only the price of computers
questions.explanation: His concern extended beyond physical danger to the meaning of human capacities.

questions.question: What is the book's stated aim?
options: Guarantee a date for general intelligence
Supply clinical treatment protocols
Provide a complete programming manual for all AI
Examine how selected AI methods work, succeed and fail
questions.explanation: Mitchell presents a critical exploration rather than a complete history or technical manual.

questions.question: What is an algorithm in simple terms?
options: A sequence of steps for solving a task
The error rate measured during testing
The final category predicted by a model
The examples used for training
questions.explanation: An algorithm is a set of instructions. A model follows computational steps to turn an input into an output.

questions.question: Why can a learned model be accurate yet difficult to explain?
options: Its predictions contain no numerical calculations
Its accuracy means every internal step is already understood
Its decision rules are spread across many learned numbers
Its training labels are always human-readable rules
questions.explanation: A model can give the right answer without offering a clear reason a person can inspect. Correctness and explainability are different qualities.

questions.question: Which four application areas are grouped together in the lecture notes?
options: Screening, transcription, voice analysis and AAC
Diagnosis, billing, drug prescribing and surgery
Translation, publishing, encryption and data storage
Screening, consent, prompting and legal review
questions.explanation: The notes group uses by what they do: flag risk, turn speech into text, examine voice signals and help communication.

questions.question: What is the trade-off when a screener catches more at-risk children but also flags unaffected children?
options: Fewer missed cases can come with more false alarms
More positive flags prove greater diagnostic certainty
Higher sensitivity always means higher specificity
A flagged child no longer needs assessment
questions.explanation: Catching more possible cases is useful, but some flags may be wrong. A follow-up assessment separates risk from diagnosis.

questions.question: Which framework do the notes mention in their discussion of high-risk medical AI?
options: BLEU
The Turing test
The EU AI Act
WordNet
questions.explanation: The notes name the EU AI Act in this context. This question checks the supplied notes, rather than giving an updated legal ruling.

questions.question: Which US body is mentioned in the notes in relation to AI in medical devices?
options: The ImageNet organizers
The FDA
The Dartmouth workshop committee
The WHO
questions.explanation: The notes connect the FDA with medical-device regulation in the United States. Legal applicability still depends on the actual device and setting.

questions.question: Which ethical idea means trying to help while avoiding harm?
options: Beneficence and non-maleficence
Exploration and exploitation
Precision and recall
Encoding and decoding
questions.explanation: Beneficence means doing good; non-maleficence means avoiding harm. The notes connect them with real-world validation and continuing checks.

questions.question: What does the WHO principle about human well-being emphasize in the notes?
options: Only the cheapest possible service
Only the highest model accuracy
Only the needs of the software developer
Safety and the public interest
questions.explanation: A useful health tool should protect people and serve their interests. A high score alone does not establish that it does so.

questions.question: What does validity mean for an AI tool in the notes?
options: It gives the same confident answer to every user
It works for the purpose it is intended to serve
It has a large number of learned weights
It is popular in many countries
questions.explanation: First ask what the tool is supposed to do. Then check whether evidence shows it can do that particular job.

questions.question: Why should checks continue after an AI tool is introduced?
options: Real patients and conditions can differ from the original study
Monitoring is needed only before the first use
One successful pilot guarantees every later result
The developer's original accuracy can never change
questions.explanation: A tool may work differently with new people or recording conditions. Continued checking helps detect those problems.

questions.question: Which follow-up best makes a technical draft easier for a caregiver to use?
options: Remove all instructions and keep only the diagnosis
Make the answer longer without changing the wording
Rewrite it in simple everyday language and explain the steps
Add more specialist terms without definitions
questions.explanation: A caregiver needs clear actions and familiar words. Rewriting for the audience can make the same activity easier to follow.

questions.question: An AI draft changes the target sound and the child's age. What type of error needs correction?
options: An example of successful de-identification
Terminology and case-detail errors
A correct clinical interpretation
A harmless format preference
questions.explanation: Check the draft against the actual session. Wrong targets or ages can make a polished note describe the wrong case.

questions.question: Which statement best explains 'AI is an umbrella term'?
options: AI means only large language models
AI means only supervised learning
AI includes several approaches, rather than one single technology
AI means only one type of neural network
questions.explanation: Think of AI as a large family. Rule-based systems, machine learning and generative tools belong to different parts of that family.

questions.question: How does the deck distinguish human clinical reasoning from AI pattern recognition?
options: Both necessarily use the same reasoning process
Clinicians combine patient context with judgment; AI computes patterns in data
AI's confidence removes the need for patient context
Human reasoning consists only of matching numerical patterns
questions.explanation: A model can find a pattern in a recording. The clinician must decide what that pattern means for this particular person.

questions.question: A post-stroke recording is analyzed without considering history or therapy notes. What should the SLP add?
options: Only a second copy of the recording
The wider clinical context before interpreting the output
An assumption that all stroke cases are identical
A decision based only on the model's confidence
questions.explanation: The deck's case includes more than speech data. History, assessment and observations help the clinician judge an AI result.

questions.question: What does shared decision-making add to SLP care?
options: The model alone selects every goal
Only the developer chooses the therapy plan
The patient's priorities and preferences inform decisions with the clinician
The patient's views are replaced by a score
questions.explanation: Care involves a person, not just a dataset. Shared decisions include what matters to that person.

questions.question: What is the difference between an AI tool and an autonomous decision-maker in the deck?
options: A tool must use written rules rather than learning
An autonomous system never needs validation
A tool supplies information for interpretation; autonomous output directly drives action
A tool always has lower accuracy
questions.explanation: The distinction is about how the output is used. Information that directly triggers action requires stronger evidence and oversight.

questions.question: Which stage comes before the AI prediction in the deck's pattern-recognition framework?
options: Making the final clinical decision
Treating the prediction as clinical truth
Signing the care plan
Processing the input to identify patterns or features
questions.explanation: The model first processes information such as a recording. It then uses patterns in that information to produce an output.

questions.question: What do labels contribute in the deck's speech-learning example?
options: They provide the patient's final treatment plan
They replace the need to test new samples
They prove the model understands all communication
They tell the model the expected category during training
questions.explanation: A label gives the learning system an example of the desired answer. Testing later checks whether it can handle new samples.

questions.question: Which simplified sequence describes the deep-learning speech example?
options: Speech signal, neural network, learned patterns, prediction
Clinical decision, voice recording, consent, neural network
Speech signal, final diagnosis, consent, prediction
Prediction, recording, final diagnosis, training label
questions.explanation: The network processes a speech signal to produce a prediction. Clinical interpretation comes after that output.

questions.question: Which task in the deck uses text summarization?
options: Creating a shorter draft from a longer language sample or document
Selecting a robot's movement by reward
Detecting edges in a photograph
Measuring jitter in a voice signal
questions.explanation: Summarization makes text shorter while trying to keep the main information. The result still needs checking for missing or changed meaning.

questions.question: Why should an SLP understand AI even without building a model?
options: To judge its claims, limits and clinical usefulness
To accept every automated recommendation
To replace every patient interaction with a score
To transfer responsibility to the developer
questions.explanation: You do not need to write the software to ask good questions about it. Understanding its limits helps you use it thoughtfully.

questions.question: A tool performs well on one clinic's adult data. What should be asked before using it with local children?
options: Is the adult accuracy repeated in the advertisement?
Does it use the word intelligent in its name?
Does it produce the same report layout?
Were similar children, languages and settings represented in validation?
questions.explanation: The new group may differ from the original one. Relevant validation helps show whether the result is likely to transfer.

questions.question: How should fluent patient-education text from an LLM be treated?
options: As a draft whose clinical statements need verification
As a final clinical judgment
As verified information because it is easy to read
As reliable evidence of understanding
questions.explanation: Easy-to-read text can still contain mistakes. Readability and accuracy must be checked separately.

questions.question: What was a central conjecture behind the Dartmouth proposal?
options: Features of intelligence could be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate them
Computers could perform only arithmetic and no other task
A single summer would provide a complete scientific definition of consciousness
Only biological neurons could ever process symbols
questions.explanation: The proposal treated intelligent behavior as something that could be studied and described. It was an ambitious starting idea, not a completed proof.

questions.question: Which four pioneers are grouped as the 'big four' in the chapter?
options: Lenat, Cope, Samuel and Bongard
Turing, Rosenblatt, LeCun and Hinton
Hubel, Wiesel, Fukushima and LeCun
McCarthy, Minsky, Newell and Simon
questions.explanation: These four helped shape the early field. The chapter connects them with the Dartmouth meeting and later AI laboratories.

questions.question: In the river-crossing GPS example, what constrains an operator?
options: A learned visual feature map
Rules defining which moves are allowed
A reward assigned only after a full game
The human meaning of the word boat alone
questions.explanation: An operator can move people, but rules restrict the move. For example, the boat's capacity limits how many can cross at once.

questions.question: How are positive and negative examples used in the perceptron example?
options: They show instances of the target category and of other categories
They are examples with high and low image brightness only
They are examples collected before and after publication
They are always correct and incorrect predictions from the same model
questions.explanation: An 8 detector needs examples of 8s and examples that are not 8s. Both help it learn where the category boundary lies.

questions.question: If the perceptron already gives the correct answer, what does the described learning rule do?
options: Removes the example from the test set
Reverses every weight
Leaves its weights and threshold unchanged for that example
Changes the correct label to another category
questions.explanation: In this simple rule, changes are driven by mistakes. A correct answer does not require a correction for that example.

questions.question: Why did the absence of a general multilayer training method matter historically?
options: It showed symbolic rules could learn without examples
It prevented computers from representing numerical inputs
It proved all multilayer networks could solve only one task
It made it hard to learn the many weights in multilayer networks
questions.explanation: Adding layers can make a model more capable in principle. Researchers still needed a practical way to train those layers.

questions.question: In the digit network, what does each output unit correspond to?
options: One hidden-layer weight
One possible digit category
One pixel location
One training image
questions.explanation: There are ten digit categories, so the example has ten outputs. The largest output indicates the predicted digit.

questions.question: What do hidden-unit activations become during a forward pass?
options: Independent test labels
A replacement for all learned weights
Inputs to units in the next layer
A new set of human-written rules
questions.explanation: Information moves forward through the layers. One layer's results help the next layer calculate its results.

questions.question: What does 'distributed' emphasize in the connectionist account?
options: Every computer must connect to the internet
A network's knowledge exists only in its output name
Knowledge is represented across a pattern of units and connections
Each concept must occupy one human-readable rule
questions.explanation: The information is spread across many numerical relationships. It is not simply a separate written fact stored in one place.

questions.question: Why are perceptual or motor tasks attractive for subsymbolic approaches in the chapter?
options: Such systems require no experience
These tasks always have only one possible input
All physical skills can be completely listed in a short rule set
People often cannot state the exact rules they use to perform them
questions.explanation: You may recognize a face or catch an object without explaining every step. Learning from examples can help where explicit rules are hard to write.

questions.question: How did MYCIN obtain much of its explicit medical knowledge?
options: Programmers interviewed expert physicians to develop rules
It clustered unlabeled photographs
It read all medical papers without human preparation
It learned by playing itself at a medical game
questions.explanation: People had to draw knowledge out of experts and encode it. This illustrates the human work behind a rule-based system.

questions.question: Why was the internet important to the later rise of machine learning?
options: It eliminated the need for computing power
It supplied far larger amounts of usable data
It solved the problem of general intelligence by itself
It made all data perfectly labeled and unbiased
questions.explanation: Learning systems need examples. Growing online collections made many more examples available, although quality and labeling still mattered.

questions.question: In the chapter's historical account, what does Moore's law describe?
options: An approximate doubling of chip components over time
A fixed number of hidden layers in every network
A guaranteed doubling of human understanding each year
A rule that every AI system is unbiased
questions.explanation: It describes a hardware trend discussed in the book. Faster hardware alone is not the same as a complete account of intelligence.

questions.question: In a doubling sequence that starts with two grains, how many are on the fourth square?
questions.explanation: The sequence is 2, 4, 8, 16. Repeated doubling grows much faster than adding the same amount each time.

questions.question: Who took opposite sides in the book's wager about a Turing test by 2029?
options: Arthur Samuel and David Cope
Marvin Minsky and Frank Rosenblatt
Yann LeCun and Fei-Fei Li
Ray Kurzweil and Mitchell Kapor
questions.explanation: Kurzweil expected a machine to pass; Kapor was skeptical. The chapter describes their historical wager and its planned deadline.

questions.question: Why did the wager specify long interviews and multiple judges?
options: To replace conversation with an image test
To guarantee that any chatbot would pass
To make the test conditions harder to satisfy with superficial tricks
To remove all human comparison
questions.explanation: The result depends on the test rules. Longer, carefully designed conversations provide a stricter challenge than brief exchanges.

questions.question: What did Kapor emphasize about learning in the wager discussion?
options: Only arithmetic speed matters to thought
Bodies, emotions and experience shape human knowledge
All important knowledge is explicitly written in books
Faster reading automatically supplies all common sense
questions.explanation: People learn through living in the world, not just reading descriptions. Kapor questioned whether text alone could supply that experience.

questions.question: What objection do the skeptics raise about extrapolating hardware growth to intelligence?
options: Hardware trends prove that brains cannot be studied
Faster chips make all learning impossible
A past forecasting success makes every later forecast certain
Software and understanding do not necessarily improve at the same exponential rate
questions.explanation: More computing power is useful. It does not by itself tell us how to build the missing abilities.

questions.question: What is occlusion in the chapter's object-recognition discussion?
options: An image having no pixels
An object changing its category label
A network having too many output units
Part of an object being hidden by something else
questions.explanation: A fence or a person can hide part of a dog. A recognizer must still deal with the incomplete view.

questions.question: What effect can prior knowledge have on human vision, according to the chapter?
options: It can influence what a person perceives
It is completely separate from perception
It removes all visual illusions
It matters only after an image has been named
questions.explanation: People do not process a picture using raw pixels alone. Expectations and knowledge also shape interpretation.

questions.question: What is the difference between feed-forward and feedback connections here?
options: Feedback means the final answer is always correct
Both always connect a network directly to its training labels
Feed-forward goes toward higher layers; feedback returns toward lower layers
Feed-forward means no intermediate computation occurs
questions.explanation: The two directions allow different flows of information. The book notes that the brain has substantial feedback connections.

questions.question: In the ConvNet example, what does an activation indicate?
options: The number of human annotators
A complete explanation of the scene's meaning
How strongly a detector responds to its input
The size of the independent test set
questions.explanation: A high activation means the unit responded strongly. It is a numerical response, not a full human-style interpretation.

questions.question: What does moving the same feature detector across an image help achieve?
options: A separate human-written rule for every pixel
Detection of a feature at different locations
A guarantee that every object is understood
Removal of all training examples
questions.explanation: An edge can occur in many places. Reusing the detector allows the model to look for it across the image.

questions.question: During ConvNet training, how are predicted category scores used?
options: Compared with target outputs to guide weight changes
Accepted as new ground-truth labels without checking
Used only to rename the input files
Stored without affecting any later calculation
questions.explanation: The model compares its output with the expected category. The error guides small changes to its weights.

questions.question: How were training and test images used in the benchmark described?
options: Training labels were hidden but test labels guided all updates
Training images supported learning; separate test images measured performance
All test images were used repeatedly to fit the model
The test set contained only correctly predicted images
questions.explanation: Keeping examples separate helps reveal whether learning works beyond the training data.

questions.question: What relationship does a WordNet chain such as cappuccino to coffee illustrate?
options: A list ordered only by word length
A more specific term linked to a broader category
A chronological list of training events
A sequence of network weight updates
questions.explanation: Cappuccino is a kind of coffee, and coffee is a kind of beverage. These category links helped organize ImageNet.

questions.question: Why was using image-search results alone insufficient for ImageNet?
options: Human checking would make the categories less meaningful
Returned pictures could be irrelevant or incorrectly matched to the noun
Every returned picture lacked any visual content
Search engines already supplied perfect task labels
questions.explanation: A search for a term can return mixed results. Human checking helped decide which pictures truly belonged.

questions.question: Why can repeated test-server submissions become a problem?
options: They let test feedback influence later model choices
They remove the need to report hyperparameters
They prove the model has learned the right concepts
They automatically add more independent test examples
questions.explanation: A test stops being a clean final check when developers keep adjusting their model to its results.

questions.question: Does a correct category prove the network used the intended object in the image?
options: No, correct categories are never useful
Yes, especially when top-5 accuracy is high
No, it may rely on another correlated part of the image
Yes, a correct label reveals the exact evidence used
questions.explanation: A correct answer can come from the wrong cue. Looking at where and why a model responds helps test this.

questions.question: What ability is needed beyond naming objects to understand a scene?
options: Only more copies of the same photograph
Only a higher score on an unchanged label task
Knowledge of relationships, events and possible intentions
Only a longer list of category names
questions.explanation: Understanding a scene includes how its parts relate. Naming dog and person does not explain what is happening between them.

questions.question: What does the learning rate control in the chapter's discussion?
options: Which clinical diagnosis is correct
How large a weight change is made during learning
How many words are in the vocabulary
How long the patient has had a difficulty
questions.explanation: The learning rate affects the size of learning steps. It is one of the settings chosen for the training process.

questions.question: Why can a robot's household photographs challenge a web-trained classifier?
options: Web images guarantee transfer to every setting
They necessarily contain new object categories only
The robot's camera removes all pixels
Their viewpoints and visual conditions differ from typical web photographs
questions.explanation: The same object may look different from a low or unusual angle. Changing the source of images can reveal weak generalization.

questions.question: In the kitchen example, why could the model confuse a man's category?
options: It learned a training-data association between kitchens and women
It applied a verified logical rule about people
It proved the kitchen caused the person's gender
It understood the person's identity from the room
questions.explanation: The model used a background association. That shortcut can create unfair errors when the association does not fit a new image.

questions.question: Why is removing one offensive category only a limited repair for a biased recognizer?
options: It does not show that other biased associations have been fixed
It guarantees equal performance for every group
It replaces the training data with a representative dataset
It explains all of the network's decisions
questions.explanation: Hiding one label may stop one visible error. The deeper problem in the data or learned patterns may remain.

questions.question: What is notable about adversarial examples that transfer between networks?
options: A change designed against one model can also fool another model
They prove that all networks have identical weights
They affect only the exact model used to create them
They require the same training images in every case
questions.explanation: Different models can share vulnerabilities. Changing the architecture alone may not remove the problem.

questions.question: Why does the book compare visual illusions with AI adversarial errors cautiously?
options: An adversarial input is necessarily visible to every human
Visual illusions show humans cannot recognize any object
Any human illusion proves every AI error is harmless
Both show errors, but the mechanisms and kinds of understanding may differ
questions.explanation: Humans can be fooled too. That fact alone does not mean a model perceives or understands a scene in the same way.

questions.question: How might AI support a person with a visual disability in the chapter's examples?
options: Read printed text or describe useful visual information
Guarantee every generated description is correct
Ensure an image contains no private information
Replace every need to check an important output
questions.explanation: Accessibility is a real benefit. It still depends on reliable output that is useful to the person.

questions.question: Why can a false face-recognition match be serious in law enforcement?
options: It is harmless if the overall accuracy is high
It always gets corrected before anyone acts
It can wrongly connect a person with suspicion or an investigation
It affects only the photograph's file size
questions.explanation: A wrong identity can have real consequences. The seriousness of the use matters alongside the average score.

questions.question: Which rights are highlighted in the face-recognition discussion?
options: Only control over image resolution
Only a right to faster computation
Privacy and freedom of expression
Only ownership of the software code
questions.explanation: Surveillance can affect how freely people move and speak. That is why the discussion includes civil rights as well as accuracy.

questions.question: Why does the book discuss the limits of industry self-regulation?
options: Only companies can understand public interests
The creators of tools should not be the only voices deciding acceptable risks
Every technical risk has already been solved
Public oversight always makes software less accurate
questions.explanation: Developers have important knowledge, but affected people and public institutions also have interests in the rules.

questions.question: What did Asimov's Runaround example demonstrate?
options: Three laws remove all ambiguity from real situations
Following simple laws can trap a robot in conflicting demands
Moral decisions can be replaced with a larger training set alone
A robot must always ignore human instructions
questions.explanation: A rule may push the robot toward one action while another rule pushes it away. Real situations can expose conflicts in simple instructions.

questions.question: What question should be asked before choosing a system's objective?
options: Will a higher number always prove the system is beneficial?
Does this measurable target actually express what people want?
Can the target be optimized without considering consequences?
Can the developer avoid stating any intended purpose?
questions.explanation: A system can optimize the wrong thing very well. Choosing the right aim is part of the value-alignment problem.

questions.question: What is an episode in the Rosie learning example?
options: One label for a speech sample
A single stored weight
The full set of every possible state
One sequence of actions ending with the task outcome or stopping point
questions.explanation: The robot tries a sequence, then tries again. Learning builds across many such episodes.

questions.question: Why does Rosie initially choose actions at random?
options: She has not yet learned which actions are valuable in each state
She already knows the shortest route to the ball
Random action guarantees an immediate reward
Her state contains a complete plan
questions.explanation: At the beginning, the action values provide little guidance. Trying actions creates experience from which to learn.

questions.question: What makes the book's Rosie state representation unusually simple?
options: It assumes she knows exactly how many steps she is from the ball
It includes every possible camera image and sound
It has no connection to the ball's location
It changes the meaning of a step after every action
questions.explanation: Real robots usually have uncertain observations. The example removes much of that difficulty so the learning idea is easier to see.

questions.question: Why might a real robot's Forward action have an uncertain result?
options: The reward always arrives before movement
All real movements have exactly the same result
Terrain or obstacles can change how far or how safely it moves
Action values cannot contain any numbers
questions.explanation: An instruction is not a guarantee of a physical outcome. The robot must handle variability in the real world.

questions.question: Why is always selecting the currently best-known action risky?
options: Exploring removes all previously learned information
The agent must ignore all its experience
An untried action might lead to a better reward
The best-known action can never succeed
questions.explanation: The current favorite may not be the true best option. Some exploration helps discover alternatives.

questions.question: Why are thousands of real-world learning trials costly?
options: They take time and can wear out or endanger physical systems
Physical trials supply perfect knowledge instantly
Robots can experience unlimited trials with no consequences
Real-world rewards are always obvious and immediate
questions.explanation: Trial and error is much cheaper in a simulation. Real machines and environments impose practical limits.

questions.question: Why were Atari games useful for comparing learning methods?
options: A common software environment allowed repeatable tests
The games directly proved clinical effectiveness
All games required the same final policy
Every game had identical rules and rewards
questions.explanation: A shared test environment makes comparison easier. Success still concerns the games tested, not every real-world task.

questions.question: In the original Atari work, what was reused across games?
options: The general architecture and settings, rather than a learned policy transferred between games
The same exact winning action sequence
One set of already learned weights for all games
A complete human strategy manual for each game
questions.explanation: The method could be reused while each game was learned afresh. Reusing a recipe is different from transferring learned knowledge.

questions.question: What is a ply in the checkers-search discussion?
options: A complete game played to the end
One player's move in the look-ahead tree
One weight update in a network
An image category in ImageNet
questions.explanation: Search can look several individual moves ahead. Counting plies makes that depth more precise.

questions.question: Why does a game tree become too large to search completely?
options: Search eliminates all branching after the first move
Each possible move leads to more possible responses
Every position has only one legal continuation
The final outcome is already known at the root
questions.explanation: Possibilities multiply at each step. Limited search and evaluation are used because exhaustive search is too expensive.

questions.question: What is self-play in the AlphaGo discussion?
options: The program reads only a fixed book of human games
A human supplies every next move during training
The learning system generates games by playing against itself
Two programs play without any later learning
questions.explanation: Self-play creates experience for training. It can improve game skill without requiring a human example for every move.

questions.question: How do the ConvNet and Monte Carlo tree search support each other in the book’s AlphaGo explanation?
options: The network guides promising moves, and search results help improve the network
The network supplies every final game result, so search is unnecessary
Search chooses moves without using any network guidance
The network and search run independently with no information exchanged
questions.explanation: The network helps the search start with promising moves. Results from the search then provide better targets for training the network.

questions.question: Why does changing a game's visual layout provide a useful test?
options: It removes the need to compare with human learning
It guarantees the model learned abstract objects
It proves the original score was calculated incorrectly
It checks whether a learned behavior survives changes irrelevant to the main task
questions.explanation: If a small layout change breaks performance, the learned skill may depend on narrow visual details.

questions.question: What is an overattribution in describing AI?
options: Using an independent test set
Comparing two different algorithms fairly
Reporting a score lower than the measured value
Crediting the system with more understanding than the evidence supports
questions.explanation: A system may behave as if it has a concept without showing that concept transfers. Descriptions should stay close to the evidence.

questions.question: Why does a successful method need comparison with simpler baselines?
options: To prove simple methods always win
To remove all need to report the data
To show that high scores automatically mean general intelligence
To show whether its added complexity actually helps on the task
questions.explanation: A complex model should earn its complexity. A simple comparison helps reveal what improvement it really provides.

questions.question: Why is it difficult to specify the reward for a household helper?
options: Every helpful action has one obvious universal score
A game score can be copied unchanged into every task
Useful behavior includes several goals and possible unwanted consequences
Household tasks have no physical uncertainty
questions.explanation: Cleaning dishes is not just maximizing one easy number. Safety, correct placement and other household needs all matter.

questions.question: Why must a dishwasher robot recognize a sponge differently from a plate?
options: The objects require different actions in the task
Every object in the sink belongs in the dishwasher
An object label always supplies a complete action plan
They are guaranteed to have different pixel colors
questions.explanation: Recognizing an object is useful only when connected with the right action. A sponge may not belong where dishes do.

questions.question: What does the chapter's comparison of games and households warn against?
options: Studying how learned skills might transfer
Assuming the same favorable conditions hold in both domains
Reporting useful game-playing results
Using simulations for any research purpose
questions.explanation: Games give clear boundaries and rules. Everyday situations often do not, so transferring a method can require major changes.

questions.question: In the restaurant story, why is praise for a burned meal understood as sarcasm?
options: The words conflict with the situation and the man's behavior
The word great always means unhappy
Any short sentence is sarcastic
A restaurant order cannot be interpreted literally
questions.explanation: Meaning depends on the situation. Positive words can express the opposite when the speaker is clearly dissatisfied.

questions.question: What does the idiom 'bent out of shape' mean in the story's context?
options: Upset or angry
Physically folded
A change in handwriting
Unable to sit in a chair
questions.explanation: An idiom cannot always be understood word by word. Context helps select its intended meaning.

questions.question: Why can one-hot encoding struggle to show similarity between two words?
options: It stores a complete definition for each word
Every word receives the same vector
Different words have separate active positions without direct semantic closeness
It automatically places synonyms next to one another
questions.explanation: A one-hot code identifies a word, but does not directly say that burger and hamburger are related.

questions.question: In a semantic space, what does closeness between word vectors aim to represent?
options: The order of publication dates
Identical spelling only
Equal numbers of letters
Related patterns of meaning or use
questions.explanation: Nearby vectors are intended to capture useful relationships. They do not guarantee the system understands each word as a person does.

questions.question: In the word2vec example, what training task helps learn word representations?
options: Copying a dictionary definition exactly
Predicting the writer's full life history
Sorting all words alphabetically
Predicting words that occur in the context of an input word
questions.explanation: Words used in similar contexts receive related learned representations. The context-prediction task produces those patterns.

questions.question: Why is solving a word-vector analogy not the same as proving broad analogy-making ability?
options: Vector arithmetic cannot produce a useful answer
Any correct vector answer proves general intelligence
All analogies have only one possible formal solution
It may reflect statistical relationships without flexible understanding across situations
questions.explanation: A relationship in word data can be useful. Human analogy also involves deciding what matters in many new kinds of situations.

questions.question: What does parallel text mean in the translation discussion?
options: Text paired with a translation of the same content
Two unrelated documents in the same language
Repeated copies of one sentence without a translation
A list of images with no captions
questions.explanation: The paired texts show how content is expressed in different languages. They supply examples for learning translation.

questions.question: Why might a translation need a different number of words from the source?
options: The decoder must delete every article
All languages use exactly the same grammar
Languages express the same meaning with different structures
A valid translation must always copy the source word count
questions.explanation: Translation aims to preserve meaning, not word count. An encoder-decoder model can handle different sequence lengths.

questions.question: What do attention mechanisms help a translation system do in the book's account?
options: Remove the need for any training examples
Replace the target language with category labels
Guarantee correct interpretation of every idiom
Focus on relevant parts of the input at different output steps
questions.explanation: Different output words may depend on different parts of the input. Attention helps the system use those parts when needed.

questions.question: Why are bilingual human raters valuable in translation evaluation?
options: They can judge any language without knowing it
They eliminate the need to sample enough translations
They can judge quality beyond exact word overlap
They always agree and never tire
questions.explanation: A good translation may use different wording from a reference. Knowledgeable readers can assess whether it still conveys the meaning.

questions.question: Why may news-style test sentences give an incomplete view of translation ability?
options: They test every possible conversational context
They may contain less ambiguity or idiomatic language than everyday communication
News sentences have no grammatical structure
Their correct translation proves reliable handling of any document
questions.explanation: Performance depends on the kinds of text tested. Clear news writing does not cover every difficulty in natural conversation.

questions.question: Why were multiple human captions used for an image in the example?
options: Five captions guarantee perfect scene understanding
Only one person could see the image at a time
Every image contains exactly five objects
Different accurate descriptions of the same image are possible
questions.explanation: People can describe different valid aspects of one picture. Multiple examples help represent that variation.

questions.question: Why did Watson's speed on the buzzer matter to its Jeopardy result?
options: Winning depended only on reading speed and no knowledge
The contest rewarded responding before the other contestants
The buzzer supplied all correct answers
Buzzer speed showed full clinical reasoning
questions.explanation: A competition measures the whole task, including timing. Its result should not be treated as a pure measure of general understanding.

questions.question: Why are many clinical questions unlike Jeopardy clues?
options: They always have one exact response in a fixed archive
They never depend on patient history
They can be uncertain, context-dependent and lack one short clean answer
They require only a faster buzzer
questions.explanation: Real care often involves weighing evidence rather than retrieving a single trivia answer.

questions.question: What did SQuAD question writers have to ensure in the original dataset?
options: The answer appeared as a span in the supplied paragraph
Every question needed a full-page explanation
The answer was deliberately missing from the text
The answer required an external clinical guideline
questions.explanation: This requirement makes the task answer extraction. It limits what a good score can tell us about broader comprehension.

questions.question: Why can changing one word alter a Winograd schema's answer?
options: The nearest noun is always the correct referent
The change alters which interpretation fits common sense
The first named person must always be the answer
The correct pronoun reference is fixed by its spelling alone
questions.explanation: A small wording change can change the likely cause or situation. Resolving the pronoun requires attention to meaning.

questions.question: When water is poured from a bottle into a cup until 'it is empty,' which container is normally meant?
options: Both containers equally
The cup
The bottle
The sentence's speaker
questions.explanation: The bottle loses water as the cup gains it. That everyday knowledge helps resolve the pronoun.

questions.question: Why are strong QA results on one benchmark insufficient for a general-comprehension claim?
options: A benchmark score contains no useful information
Another task may require reasoning the benchmark did not test
All reading tasks are equivalent
Matching human performance proves every form of language understanding
questions.explanation: A test samples particular abilities. A strong result should be described within that scope.

questions.question: What does understanding cause and effect add beyond noticing correlation?
options: An explanation of why one event brings about another
Proof that any frequent pattern is causal
A guarantee that all future events are certain
A rule that related events always cause each other
questions.explanation: Two events can occur together without one causing the other. Causal understanding concerns how an event produces a change.

questions.question: Why does predicting a pedestrian's next action involve more than object recognition?
options: Only image brightness determines a person's intention
It requires thinking about goals, attention and likely behavior
All pedestrians move in exactly the same way
Naming the person supplies every future action
questions.explanation: Seeing a person is one step. Predicting what they might do requires a richer model of the situation.

questions.question: How does mental simulation differ from simply recalling one past scene?
options: It must reproduce every past detail exactly
It cannot include possible future events
It can combine experience to imagine a new possible situation
It always supplies a certain prediction
questions.explanation: People can use what they know to imagine what might happen next, even when the exact situation is new.

questions.question: What everyday expression illustrates the time-as-money metaphor?
options: The screen has many pixels
I spent too much time on it
The cup contains warm water
The dog crossed the road
questions.explanation: The word spent usually concerns money, but is also used for time. The chapter uses such expressions to discuss abstract thought.

questions.question: Why can a child recognize a cartoon cat after seeing real cats?
options: The cartoon must have exactly the same pixels as a real cat
Only a printed category label allows recognition
The child can connect different appearances to a broader category
The child needs a separate rule for every possible drawing
questions.explanation: Abstraction allows a category to extend beyond one exact appearance. A real animal and a drawing can share the relevant idea.

questions.question: In the legal analogy, why compare a blogging platform with a wall carrying graffiti?
options: A visual match proves the entire legal argument
The platform and wall have identical physical materials
The proposed similarity concerns responsibility for other people's writing
Every property of a wall must transfer to a website
questions.explanation: The analogy maps a relevant relationship, not every surface detail. Whether such a legal analogy succeeds still depends on the case.

questions.question: How can Cyc infer a new assertion from existing ones?
options: Only by receiving a reward after physical movement
Only by counting image pixels
By applying logical relations to stored knowledge
Only by generating random text
questions.explanation: If the stored rules and facts support a conclusion, an inference procedure can derive it. This is different from learning only numerical associations.

questions.question: Why is twelve-example learning important in the Bongard discussion?
options: It guarantees every neural network can learn the rule perfectly
It shows that training data quality is irrelevant
It highlights how people can identify an abstract distinction from few cases
It removes the need to decide which attributes matter
questions.explanation: People often infer the relevant relationship quickly. The challenge is to give machines similarly flexible learning, not just more examples.

questions.question: If azbzczd becomes abcd, what analogous result is described for pxqxrxsxt?
options: pqrsxt
abcd
pqrst
pxqxrxsxt
