questions.explanation: The repeated z and x characters play the same role: extra letters to remove. Recognizing that role reveals the remaining sequence.

questions.question: If abc becomes abd, what answer does the book discuss for ace using a double-successor pattern?
options: bdf
acf
acg
abd
questions.explanation: In ace the letters advance by two. Extending that pattern changes the final e to g rather than simply to the next alphabet letter.

questions.question: What would self-monitoring help a problem-solving program notice?
options: That its training data contain no possible bias
That it keeps repeating an unsuccessful approach
That all tasks use the same representation
That every generated answer is automatically valid
questions.explanation: A solver can waste effort repeating a failed strategy. Monitoring its own actions could help it change approach.

questions.question: What makes the photograph of a foot on a weighing scale difficult to understand fully?
options: It contains no relationships between people
It can be explained from the photograph's file name alone
It requires only naming the scale
It requires physical and social knowledge to recognize the trick and the amusement
questions.explanation: A foot adds weight, the person may not notice, and observers understand the joke. Those connected inferences go beyond listing objects.

questions.question: What responsibility does the book's level 3 summary retain for the human driver?
options: At level 3 the vehicle works in every possible condition
At level 3 no human can ever take control
At level 3 the vehicle provides no steering assistance
Remain attentive and ready to take control when requested
questions.explanation: The supplied book says the human must remain attentive and ready to take over. This question follows its historical summary, rather than giving current driving guidance.

questions.question: What distinguishes level 4 from level 5 in the book's summary?
options: Level 4 has no autonomous operation at all
Level 5 controls speed only
The levels differ only in the number of passengers
Level 4 is limited to certain conditions; level 5 covers all conditions in the definition
questions.explanation: The operating limits are crucial. A system working within a defined domain should not be described as working everywhere.

questions.question: Why might predictable human behavior still be hard for an autonomous car to rely on?
options: A high-definition map includes every future human action
People can act unexpectedly, break rules or deliberately test the vehicle
Geofencing removes all interactions with people
Every pedestrian always follows the same rules
questions.explanation: A mapped area still contains people. Maps do not guarantee how those people will behave.

questions.question: How did human judgment guide the genetic-art example?
options: Only numerical image size determined which work was best
People selected preferred outputs from generated variations
The program proved its own artistic value without human judgment
Every random output was accepted as equally successful
questions.explanation: Generating options and judging their value are different activities. Human selection shaped the artistic results discussed.

questions.question: Why does the author question the idea of an all-knowing, instantly learning superintelligence?
options: A chess-playing program cannot use numerical memory
All intelligent programs must have the same speed as a brain
Human intelligence may be closely tied to embodied experience and cognitive limits
The book proves that no machine can perform arithmetic
questions.explanation: The author asks whether features treated as human limitations also help make broad intelligence possible. This is an argument, not a settled proof.

questions.question: What does the final discussion say about the original Dartmouth research questions?
options: Every listed question has been completely solved
The original proposal concerned no topic relevant to AI
Only faster hardware remains to be developed
Many remain important and unresolved despite major progress
questions.explanation: Progress can be substantial while deep questions remain open. The book ends by returning to learning, reasoning, language and creativity.

questions.question: What is the main documentation benefit proposed in the new lecture?
options: A final note that needs no source checking
An automatic replacement for clinical judgment
A guarantee that every session detail is correct
A faster structured first draft for clinician review
questions.explanation: The tool can help organize a draft quickly. The clinician still checks whether the draft matches the session.

questions.question: Why can a fluent AI-generated note be misleading?
options: Professional wording can hide factual and numerical errors
Only poorly written notes need verification
A polished note cannot contain missing information
Fluency proves the system observed the session
questions.explanation: Good writing and accurate content are different things. Check the evidence even when a note sounds professional.

questions.question: Which task fits the lecture's account of an LLM's useful role?
options: Seeing an unmentioned gesture from text alone
Accepting responsibility for the signed note
Extracting supplied details into a requested table
Knowing an unrecorded caregiver report
questions.explanation: An LLM can reorganize information it receives. It cannot recover an event that was never included in its input.

questions.question: Which documentation burden does the lecture identify alongside time and consistency?
options: Removing the need for patient history
Tabulating trial-by-trial data
Selecting a diagnosis from every recording
Making every note the same length
questions.explanation: Many individual responses take time to count and organize. AI may help with a first pass, but the counts need checking.

questions.question: In the lecture's six-step workflow, which two steps explicitly use AI?
options: Choosing the clinical goal and approving the plan
Reviewing the evidence and accepting professional responsibility
Transcribing speech and drafting the SOAP note
Obtaining consent and signing the note
questions.explanation: Speech-to-text produces a raw transcript, and the LLM produces a draft. The surrounding preparation and review remain clinician-owned.

questions.question: Which step follows raw transcription and precedes LLM drafting?
options: Prepare the transcript by de-identifying and labeling it
Sign and file the final note
Remove all prompt-level information
Accept the first generated diagnosis
questions.explanation: A raw transcript may lack important context or contain identifiers. Prepare it before asking the LLM to draft the note.

questions.question: Why should speaker labels appear on each transcript turn?
options: To replace the need to record non-verbal actions
To make every statement count as a caregiver report
To turn a transcript into a diagnosis
To distinguish who said each statement
questions.explanation: Labels such as therapist, child and parent help prevent statements being attributed to the wrong person.

questions.question: What do T, C and P mean in the lecture's transcript speaker labels?
options: Therapist, child and parent
Training, classification and prediction
Target, correct and prompted
Trial, clinician and plan
questions.explanation: These labels identify speakers in this transcript. Their meaning depends on context, so do not confuse speaker P with a prompt code.

questions.question: How should Urdu–English code-switching be handled when preparing the transcript?
options: Preserve the utterance as spoken and add a meaning gloss where needed
Change the child's words into a more advanced sentence
Translate everything silently and delete the original
Mark every Urdu word as an error
questions.explanation: Keep the actual language sample available for checking. A gloss explains meaning without replacing what was said.

questions.question: What does 'type the invisible' mean in this lecture?
options: Remove all gestures from the clinical record
Ask the LLM to infer everything missing from the audio
Write non-verbal actions and prompts in brackets
Guess the child's unspoken intentions
questions.explanation: A text model cannot see a gesture that is absent from the transcript. Add relevant actions explicitly, such as an AAC button press.

questions.question: Which transcript entry best records a non-verbal support event?
options: The model should decide whether a gesture happened
The child probably understood the task
No prompt was recorded, so no prompt occurred
[Therapist points to the AAC WANT button]
questions.explanation: Describe the observed action directly. This lets a later reviewer distinguish independent performance from prompted performance.

questions.question: Why should trials be numbered before asking AI to code them?
options: Numbering guarantees that all codes are correct
Each numbered trial automatically becomes independent
Each response and code can be matched and checked
Numbering makes response evidence unnecessary
questions.explanation: Trial numbers give the reviewer a clear reference. They also help reveal missing or invented trials.

questions.question: In the fictional Child A case, what is the target skill?
options: Understanding a paragraph read aloud
Two-word requests using want plus an object
Independent three-word descriptions
Accurate production of one speech sound
questions.explanation: The goal is a two-word request. A response must be judged against that goal, rather than against word production in general.

questions.question: What does age 5;2 mean in the fictional case?
options: Two years and five months
Five years and two weeks
Five and a half years exactly
Five years and two months
questions.explanation: The notation separates years and months. Accurate age information helps keep the documentation tied to the right case.

questions.question: Why must the six-trial excerpt not be presented as the entire twenty-trial session?
options: All twenty trials necessarily had the same outcomes
The six trials contain no measurable data
A sample percentage automatically describes every planned trial
The remaining fourteen trials are not supplied in the excerpt
questions.explanation: The lecture supplies six of twenty planned trials. Report what the excerpt actually supports instead of inventing the other results.

questions.question: Which letters form the documentation-prompt mnemonic in the new lecture?
options: R-A-S-P-T
I-P-M-G-V
S-O-A-P-C
R-C-T-F-C
questions.explanation: The mnemonic stands for Role, Context, Task, Format and Constraints. It helps organize a clear drafting request.

questions.question: What role is specified for the LLM in the new documentation prompt?
options: Substitute for the signing professional
Independent diagnosing clinician
Unsupervised care-plan decision-maker
Documentation assistant for an SLP
questions.explanation: The role narrows the request to drafting support. It does not give the model professional responsibility.

questions.question: Which details belong in Context for the lecture's documentation prompt?
options: Only the final note headings
Age, goal, session type, languages and AAC availability
Only the instruction to avoid invention
Only the number of words in the answer
questions.explanation: Context tells the model the relevant background. The task and constraints then explain what it should do with that information.

questions.question: What source restriction does the lecture's prompt impose?
options: Use only the transcript and the coded data table
Add common caregiver concerns from memory
Use a likely diagnosis to complete the note
Fill gaps using similar patients' histories
questions.explanation: Limiting the source reduces unsupported additions. The clinician still checks whether the model followed the instruction.

questions.question: Why does the prompt ask the LLM to copy numbers from a verified table?
options: To keep note writing separate from checked coding and arithmetic
To prevent the clinician from inspecting the counts
To make trial-level data unnecessary
To treat the LLM's first calculation as final
questions.explanation: The clinician verifies the counts first. The drafting step then uses those numbers instead of asking the LLM to recalculate them.

questions.question: What should the prompt require when a detail is absent?
options: Write [NOT STATED]
Treat the missing detail as a normal finding
Supply the most typical detail
Copy a detail from another session
questions.explanation: A visible missing-data marker is more honest than a plausible guess. It tells the clinician what needs attention.

questions.question: How should an ambiguous transcript detail be handled in the constrained prompt?
options: Convert it into a definite clinical finding
Choose the most reassuring interpretation
Flag it for clinician review
Delete all evidence that the ambiguity existed
questions.explanation: An uncertain detail should stay visibly uncertain. The clinician decides how to resolve it.

questions.question: Which format does the documentation prompt request?
options: S, O, A and P headings with short bullets
One uninterrupted narrative without headings
Only a diagnostic label and a confidence score
A table containing no source information
questions.explanation: The specified headings make the note easier to review. A clear structure does not by itself guarantee accurate content.

questions.question: What is the specific risk in the Subjective section shown in the new lecture?
options: Mixing hidden-layer activations with output labels
Recording an actual client statement with its speaker
Using a prompt level in a trial table
Inventing a caregiver report that was never recorded
questions.explanation: Subjective statements still need a source. Do not write that a parent said something when the transcript contains no such report.

questions.question: What is the specific Objective-section risk highlighted by the lecture?
options: Including measurable trial results
Giving the number of observed trials
Showing both correct and independent performance
Wrong counts and missing prompt information
questions.explanation: A note can overstate skill when it changes the counts or hides the support the child needed.

questions.question: Why do Assessment and Plan need the clinician's authorship or approval?
options: They can be approved by fluent wording alone
They contain clinical interpretation and decisions about next steps
They are only direct quotations from the transcript
They never require evidence
questions.explanation: The clinician decides what the results mean and what should happen next. A drafting tool does not take over that judgment.

questions.question: What should caregiver consent address in the lecture's workflow?
options: Only the final note's spelling
Recording and the use of AI to process the material
Only whether a transcript has speaker labels
Only permission to create an anonymous filename
questions.explanation: Caregivers should understand both recording and processing. Follow the institution's consent procedure.

questions.question: Which extra tool-policy detail does the new lecture ask clinicians to check?
options: Data-retention and training settings
Only whether the interface has dark mode
Only how long the vendor's name is
Only the number of formatting templates
questions.explanation: Know what happens to the submitted material and how long it is retained. Use an institution-approved tool.

questions.question: Why does the lecture suggest keeping versions of useful prompts?
options: So all later patients receive an identical plan
So old prompts can replace source transcripts
So changes to drafting instructions can be tracked and reviewed
So the newest prompt can bypass clinical review
questions.explanation: A version record helps show which instructions produced a draft. It supports review and improvement of the workflow.

questions.question: When should the final note be signed and filed in the six-step workflow?
options: As soon as all four headings are present
After the clinician reviews, corrects and completes it
Immediately after the LLM returns its first draft
Before trial data are checked
questions.explanation: Signing comes after review. The professional accepting the note is responsible for its contents.

questions.question: Why does a supported-correct percentage alone give an incomplete picture of skill?
options: It removes the need to record no-response trials
It proves the child has mastered the skill independently
It always undercounts independent responses
It can hide how much prompting was needed
questions.explanation: A child can be correct with considerable help. Track correctness and independence separately to see the difference.

questions.question: According to the lecture's planning matrix, what should follow correct independent performance?
options: Plan generalisation to other situations
Increase physical prompting on every trial
Classify the successful response as an error
Automatically increase every target to three words
questions.explanation: The child can perform without extra help on that trial. The lecture then points toward checking use beyond that exact situation.

questions.question: What does the planning matrix recommend for correct but prompted performance?
options: Immediately declare independent mastery
Delete the successful trial
Stop tracking the type of support
Systematically fade prompts
questions.explanation: The response is successful but still depends on help. Fading prompts aims to make it more independent.

questions.question: What does the planning matrix recommend for an incorrect response without a prompt?
options: Record independent mastery
Analyze the error pattern
Assume the transcript is missing a correct response
Add the response to the prompted-correct total
questions.explanation: An error can reveal what is difficult. Examine its pattern instead of treating any independent attempt as a success.

questions.question: What does the matrix suggest when a response remains incorrect even with prompting?
options: Count it as correct because help was provided
Increase the independent-accuracy numerator
Remove it from all trial totals
Simplify the task or change the prompt
questions.explanation: Support did not produce the target response. The lecture suggests adjusting the demand or the help offered.

questions.question: How should no response be treated in the lecture's data system?
options: Automatically merged with prompted-correct responses
Recorded separately as NR
Assumed to be an independent success
Omitted from the total without explanation
questions.explanation: NR makes a distinct outcome visible. It remains part of the total trial count used in the worked calculations.

questions.question: What must clinicians specify before human or AI coding begins?
options: Only the number of paragraphs in the note
Only the model's preferred diagnosis
The coding rules, wait time and scoring approach
Only a desired final percentage
questions.explanation: Decide the rules first so both coders judge the same behavior in the same way.

questions.question: In this lecture's coding key, what qualifies for I+?
options: Any final correct response after a model
A correct response on the first opportunity without a prompt
No response within the wait time
Any response containing one relevant word
questions.explanation: I+ means the target was correct without additional help on that opportunity. A later success after prompting belongs elsewhere.

questions.question: What additional information should accompany a P+ code?
options: A replacement for the original response
The level of prompt that produced the correct response
An invented independent score
The child's presumed diagnosis
questions.explanation: P+ tells you help was needed. The prompt level tells you what kind of help led to success.

questions.question: Which prompt code identifies a verbal cue in the new lecture?
options: M
G
V
P
questions.explanation: V stands for a verbal cue, such as beginning the request with I want. It is different from giving a full model.

questions.question: Which prompt code identifies a complete model such as 'Want car'?
options: V
G
M
P
questions.explanation: M marks a modeled response for the child to repeat. The record should show that the successful response followed this support.

questions.question: Which prompt code applies to pointing at an AAC button?
options: V
G
P
M
questions.explanation: G represents a gestural or visual prompt. The AAC press can be correct while still depending on that cue.

questions.question: Which prompt code represents physical guidance in this lecture?
options: G
M
P
V
questions.explanation: P identifies physical support, such as hand-over-hand guidance in the lecture's example. Record the support actually used.

questions.question: In the fictional case, 'Want bubble' follows the ordinary task question without an extra cue. What code does the lecture assign?
options: P+ with M
NR
Incorrect
I+
questions.explanation: The target two-word request is produced without an additional prompt. The lecture codes this trial as independently correct.

questions.question: A child first says 'Car' and then says 'Want car' after the therapist models it. How is this trial coded in the lecture?
options: P+ with M
NR
I+
P+ with G
questions.explanation: The initial one-word response did not meet the target. The two-word success followed a model, so it is prompted-correct.

questions.question: A two-word request is the target, but the child says 'No.' Which code is assigned in the worked case?
options: Incorrect
I+
NR
P+ with V
questions.explanation: The child responded, so this is not NR. The response does not meet the specified two-word requesting target.

questions.question: In the case, 'Want ball' is produced without an extra cue. Which code does the lecture give?
options: NR
I+
P+ with G
P+ with M
questions.explanation: The response meets the goal without an additional prompt. It is the second independent success in the excerpt.

questions.question: The therapist points to WANT and the child presses WANT plus JUICE on AAC. What is the case's coding?
options: P+ with G
Incorrect because only speech can meet the case target
I+ simply because AAC was used
NR because there was no spoken answer
questions.explanation: The lecture accepts this AAC request as correct. It remains prompted because the therapist provided a gestural cue.

questions.question: A child gives no response within the case's five-second wait. What is the appropriate code?
options: NR
P+ with G
P+ with M
I+
questions.explanation: NR records the absence of a response within the chosen wait period. Do not invent an answer to complete the trial.

questions.question: What is the tally for the lecture's six-trial case?
options: 1 I+, 3 P+, 0 incorrect and 2 NR
2 I+, 1 P+, 2 incorrect and 1 NR
4 I+, 0 P+, 1 incorrect and 1 NR
2 I+, 2 P+, 1 incorrect and 1 NR
questions.explanation: Two successes were independent and two needed prompts. The other outcomes were one incorrect response and one no response.

questions.question: For 2 I+, 2 P+, 1 incorrect and 1 NR, what is total correctness with any support?
options: 4/6, about 67%
2/6, about 33%
questions.explanation: Add independent and prompted successes, then divide by all six trials. The result describes success with any support.

questions.question: For the six-trial case, why should 67% not be labeled independent performance?
options: All four correct responses were unprompted
NR must be counted as independent success
Two of the four correct responses needed prompts
Percentages cannot describe independent responses
questions.explanation: Only two of the six responses were independently correct. Calling all four independent hides the extra help.

questions.question: Why should a result include n as well as a percentage?
options: It identifies the number of neural layers
It replaces the need to show the numerator
It guarantees that every trial was independent
It shows how many trials the percentage is based on
questions.explanation: The same percentage can come from very different amounts of evidence. Giving the trial count makes the result easier to interpret.

questions.question: In the three-session example, supported correctness rises 50%, 65%, 70% while independence rises 20%, 30%, 40%. What does this show?
options: Both improve, but some success still depends on prompts
Seventy percent of responses are independently correct in session 3
The two measures are interchangeable
Prompt dependence has disappeared
questions.explanation: Improvement in total correctness does not mean every success is independent. Both lines are needed to see progress clearly.

questions.question: In the illustrative third session, 14 of 20 responses are correct and 8 are independent. How many correct responses were prompted?
questions.explanation: Subtract the eight independent successes from fourteen total successes. Six correct responses still needed support.

questions.question: What trial-level evidence should an AI coding table provide?
options: Only an inferred description of motivation
Only an overall confidence statement
The exact transcript line supporting each code
Only the final percentage
questions.explanation: A source line lets the clinician check a code quickly. It makes the table easier to audit than an unsupported summary.

questions.question: Why does the lecture's AI-coding request prohibit percentages?
options: Percentages are never useful in documentation
Codes are checked first and arithmetic is done separately
A model's counts cannot be inspected by a human
Every clinical percentage should be estimated from memory
questions.explanation: Separate the coding task from calculation. Use the verified counts for arithmetic in a spreadsheet or by hand.

questions.question: What should an AI coder write when it cannot confidently classify a trial?
options: UNSURE
I+ by default
P+ by default
A likely diagnosis
questions.explanation: An uncertainty marker makes the difficulty visible. The clinician can then check the original evidence and decide.

questions.question: What is the danger of scoring only the final response after assistance?
options: It can hide an unsuccessful first attempt and overstate independence
It always lowers supported correctness to zero
It guarantees fair comparison with first-response coding
It makes prompt-level recording unnecessary
questions.explanation: A correct answer at the end may have required help. Keep the first response and any later prompted success visible.

questions.question: What check helps detect invented or skipped trials in a complete coded dataset?
options: Reconcile the number of coded trials with the source and expected trial count
Accept a total because its percentage is round
Count only rows labeled I+
Remove NR outcomes until the counts match
questions.explanation: Every coded row should match a real recorded trial. For a supplied excerpt, check its actual size rather than inventing missing session trials.

questions.question: In the five-trial activity, the child says 'Truck, truck, truck' when a two-word request is required. What is the answer-key code?
options: Incorrect
P+ with M
I+ because three words were spoken
NR
questions.explanation: Repeating one word does not produce the required want-plus-object request. Judge the target, not just the number of spoken tokens.

questions.question: What tally does the five-trial activity's answer key give?
options: 3 I+, 0 P+, 1 incorrect and 1 NR
1 I+, 1 P+, 2 incorrect and 1 NR
1 I+, 2 P+, 1 incorrect and 1 NR
2 I+, 2 P+, 1 incorrect and 0 NR
questions.explanation: The activity includes one independent success, a modeled success, an error, no response and a gesturally prompted AAC success.

questions.question: For 1 I+, 2 P+, 1 incorrect and 1 NR, what is correctness with any support?
options: 2/3, about 67%
questions.explanation: There are three correct responses altogether. Divide three by all five trials to obtain 60%.

questions.question: For 1 I+, 2 P+, 1 incorrect and 1 NR, what is independent accuracy?
options: 2/3, about 67%
1/3, about 33%
questions.explanation: Only the one I+ response was independent. Divide one by the five total trials.

questions.question: For 1 I+, 2 P+, 1 incorrect and 1 NR, what is prompt dependence among correct responses?
options: 2/3, about 67%
questions.explanation: Two of the three successful responses needed a prompt. The denominator is all correct responses, rather than all trials.

questions.question: An AI note invents a parent report absent from the transcript. Which error type best describes this?
options: Correct attribution
Supported interpretation
Fabrication
Omission
questions.explanation: The note adds information with no source. Remove it rather than treating a plausible report as something that happened.

questions.question: An AI note labels four supported successes as four independent successes. Which error type is central?
options: Accurate summarization
Data distortion
Privacy protection
Correct speaker attribution
questions.explanation: The underlying category has changed. The count of successes may be four, but the count of independent successes is only two in the case.

questions.question: An AI note mentions an AAC response but leaves out the gestural prompt. What error type is highlighted?
options: Appropriate de-identification
Correct diagnosis
Omission
A fully complete Objective section
questions.explanation: The missing prompt changes how the reader interprets the skill. Add the observed support instead of presenting the response without it.

questions.question: The AI labels requested repetition of a clinician's model as delayed echolalia. What error is highlighted by the lecture?
options: A valid independent response code
An acceptable plan change
Terminology error
A correct source quotation
questions.explanation: For this trial, the child repeated a model on request. The lecture's correction uses imitation rather than the unsupported label.

questions.question: An AI note diagnoses a disorder and says 'good progress' from the short excerpt alone. Which error type is emphasized?
options: Correct use of a glossary
Simple omission of a heading
Accurate counting
Over-interpretation
questions.explanation: The draft goes beyond what the supplied evidence supports. The clinician must judge interpretation using appropriate assessment evidence.

questions.question: An AI note assigns a therapist's statement to the parent. Which error category applies?
options: Accurate summarization
Prompt fading
Data minimization
Attribution error
questions.explanation: The content is assigned to the wrong speaker. Clear speaker labels and source checks help catch this.

questions.question: What should replace the invented home-improvement report in the audited example?
options: An inferred claim that the parent agreed with the plan
A statement that caregiver information is not stated in the source
A confident assumption of no home difficulties
A different typical report from a similar child
questions.explanation: Do not replace one invention with another. State the source's information gap honestly.

questions.question: What support detail should be added to the note about the case's AAC trial?
options: The child used the device without any support
The therapist gave physical guidance on every trial
The therapist pointed to the WANT button before the response
The device supplied a diagnosis
questions.explanation: The source records a gestural cue. That detail is needed to explain why the trial is prompted-correct.

questions.question: Why is the proposed move to three-word phrases unsupported in the unreviewed draft?
options: The original target was already three-word phrases
Every AAC response automatically requires a harder target
All six trials were independently correct
The excerpt still shows emerging two-word requests with prompt dependence
questions.explanation: A plan should follow the evidence. The lecture's corrected example continues the two-word target and works on reducing support.

questions.question: In the lecture's terminology refresher, receptive language concerns what?
options: Only voice quality
Only articulating speech sounds
Producing language
Understanding language
questions.explanation: Receptive relates to what a person understands. Keep this distinct from the language they produce.

questions.question: In the same refresher, expressive language concerns what?
options: Measuring vocal loudness only
Recognizing another person's face
Producing language
Understanding language only
questions.explanation: Expressive relates to communicating language outwardly. The term should not be substituted for receptive understanding.

questions.question: Which distinction does the lecture make between speech and language?
options: Speech means understanding and language means only voice
Language refers only to the number of syllables
Speech and language always mean exactly the same thing
Speech concerns sounds, fluency and voice; language concerns form, content and use
questions.explanation: A problem with language should not automatically be called a speech-sound problem. Precise terms help the note describe the actual target.

questions.question: What does spontaneous mean in the lecture's terminology comparison?
options: Self-initiated
Produced only after a question or stimulus
Repeated only after a model
Missing from the transcript
questions.explanation: Spontaneous describes initiation. It should not be used just because a response was spoken clearly.

questions.question: A child responds to a clinician's question without an extra model. Can that response be both elicited and independently correct under the case rules?
options: No, every elicited response must be P+
No, every correct response is spontaneous
Yes, elicited describes the situation while I+ describes additional support
Yes, but only if the response is omitted from the data
questions.explanation: The ordinary question elicits the request, while an extra cue would make it prompted in this coding system. These labels describe different aspects of a response.

questions.question: Why should an observational impression not automatically become a diagnosis?
options: Diagnosis requires appropriate assessment evidence
One successful trial establishes the whole disorder profile
Any grammatical clinical sentence is diagnostic evidence
An LLM role instruction establishes a diagnosis
questions.explanation: A note can describe observed behavior without making a diagnostic claim. The clinician needs appropriate evidence for that stronger conclusion.

questions.question: What prompt resource does the lecture suggest for improving terminology consistency?
options: An invented list of clinical definitions
Only a vendor's promotional description
The department's glossary
An unrelated patient's final report
questions.explanation: A shared glossary tells the drafting tool which terms to use. The clinician still checks that each term fits the actual case.

questions.question: What are the five review checks in the new documentation lecture?
options: Source, numbers, terms, reasoning and privacy
Input, hidden layer, output, weights and threshold
Role, task, context, examples and format
Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision and AUC
questions.explanation: This checklist is for reviewing a drafted note. Do not confuse it with prompt components or model-performance metrics.

questions.question: What does the documentation review's Source check require?
options: Every paragraph sounds plausible
Every missing detail is silently filled
Every statement can be traced to the transcript or clinical notes
The AI repeats its claim when asked again
questions.explanation: A statement needs a traceable basis. Repetition or confident wording does not provide one.

questions.question: What does the documentation review's Number check require?
options: Keep every percentage if it is neatly rounded
Drop incorrect trials before calculating accuracy
Re-tally the data and reconcile trial totals
Accept the model's arithmetic as independent verification
questions.explanation: Return to the trial records and count again. Make sure the total describes the actual dataset or excerpt.

questions.question: What does the Reasoning check protect in the new lecture?
options: The model's right to sign the note
The clinician's judgment in Assessment and Plan
Only the spelling of the heading names
Only the number of sentences in Objective
questions.explanation: Assessment interprets results and Plan sets next steps. The clinician must own those judgments.

questions.question: Which wording should raise suspicion when the evidence is limited?
options: An explicit count linked to the trial table
Excellent progress with a definite diagnosis never supplied by the clinician
A visible [NOT STATED] marker for missing information
A description of the actual prompt used
questions.explanation: Praise and certainty can disguise unsupported interpretation. Treat them as a reason to check the evidence.

questions.question: Why are round or perfect percentages a review flag rather than proof of error?
options: A rounded number proves all responses were independent
All round percentages are mathematically impossible
They should prompt a count check, but can sometimes be correct
A perfect score can be accepted without its denominator
questions.explanation: A suspicious pattern calls for checking. Decide whether the number is right from the source data, not its appearance alone.

questions.question: Which Objective entry most faithfully describes the six-trial excerpt?
options: 2 independent, 2 prompted-correct, 1 incorrect, 1 NR; 4/6 total correct
6 independent successes because twenty trials were planned
4 independent, 0 prompted-correct, 1 incorrect, 1 NR
4/6 independent with all prompt information omitted
questions.explanation: The corrected note keeps all four outcome groups visible. It distinguishes two independent successes from four total successes.

questions.question: What does the corrected Assessment say about the two-word skill?
options: It proves a new diagnosis from the excerpt alone
It is fully mastered independently
It shows that prompts are no longer relevant
It is emerging and half the correct responses still needed a prompt
questions.explanation: Two of four correct responses were prompted. The assessment describes that pattern without claiming unsupported mastery.

questions.question: What plan is given in the lecture's corrected case note?
options: Discontinue all AAC support immediately
End assessment because 67% proves independence
Continue two-word requests, fade model and gestural prompts, and reassess
Automatically introduce three-word requests at the next session
questions.explanation: This is the lecture's worked-case plan. It follows the recorded support needs rather than the unreviewed draft's unsupported escalation.

questions.question: Who owns responsibility for every word when the clinician signs an AI-assisted note?
options: The signing clinician
Only the transcription vendor
Only the caregiver
The language model
questions.explanation: A drafting tool does not take professional responsibility. The clinician must accept the final content after checking it.

questions.question: What equity risk does the lecture highlight for Urdu–English bilingual children?
options: A language difference may be wrongly recorded as a disorder
A language difference must be removed from the transcript
English-dominant training guarantees equal performance in every language
Any code-switching proves a disorder
questions.explanation: Language background affects interpretation. Preserve the child's language and avoid converting difference into an unsupported diagnostic claim.

questions.question: What transparency practice supports later auditing of AI-assisted documentation?
options: Hide how the note was drafted
Keep only the most polished sentence
Follow disclosure policy and retain prompts and versions as required
Delete the original evidence immediately
questions.explanation: A record of the process helps explain how a draft was produced and reviewed. Follow institutional requirements for disclosure and retention.

questions.question: According to the lecture, what should caregivers understand about recording and notes?
options: That the model assumes all clinical responsibility
Only the final document's color scheme
That a pseudonym guarantees complete anonymity
How AI processing is used within the approved workflow
questions.explanation: Consent and transparency include explaining processing in an understandable way. The institution's policy guides the actual process.

questions.question: What is the central two-metric rule repeated at the end of the lecture?
options: Report only the larger of the two percentages
Combine prompted and independent responses as independent
Report only the number of independent successes without a denominator
Track total correctness and independence, and report the trial count
questions.explanation: The two measures answer different questions. Giving n keeps their evidence base visible.

questions.question: What does the take-home task use as its session source?
options: A fully invented final note with no transcript
A ten-minute de-identified role-play
Only a published diagnostic label
A real identifiable patient recording sent to any public chatbot
questions.explanation: The assignment uses a role-play to practice the workflow. It still requires an appropriate transcript and constrained prompt.

questions.question: How should students assess the AI's coding in the take-home task?
options: Code the trials themselves and compare agreement with the AI
Ignore every uncertain trial
Compare only the length of the two tables
Accept the AI as the answer key without checking
questions.explanation: Independent human coding provides something to compare with the model's table. Disagreements should be examined against the source.

questions.question: If human and AI codes match on 8 of 10 compared trials, what is simple percent agreement?
questions.explanation: Divide eight matching codes by ten compared trials and multiply by 100. This exercise applies the assignment's agreement task.

questions.question: Does high human–AI coding agreement by itself prove the codes are valid?
options: Yes, agreement guarantees clinical truth
No, agreement can never be useful
Yes, any matching code removes the need for a source
No, both coders could make the same error
questions.explanation: Agreement shows how often the codes match. Accuracy still needs a check against the actual trial and the agreed rules.

questions.question: What should the assignment's error log and reflection help the student examine?
options: Only which tool had the most attractive interface
Which errors occurred, their types and how the student corrected them
Only the final percentage with all disagreements removed
Only whether the AI wrote more words than a human
questions.explanation: Logging errors makes the review process visible. Reflection should connect those errors with better checking and documentation decisions.
